title: Module Overview
content:
## Why this module matters

![A historic survey party in the field. Surveying has always paired careful field observation with disciplined measurement and record-keeping — the same foundation the FS exam tests.](/lessons/fs/photos/m1-survey-crew.jpg "Photo: Elias Olcott Beaman / James Fennemore / John… — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons")

The NCEES FS exam blends two knowledge areas that this module covers head-on: **Applied Mathematics and Statistics** (10–15 questions) and **Surveying Principles** (13–20 questions, the measurement-theory half). Together with the measurement-science questions embedded in **Survey Computations** (17–26), the material here is worth roughly **15% of your score** and — just as important — underpins every other computation in the course. You cannot reduce a traverse, balance a level loop, or judge whether a measurement is acceptable without understanding error.

Everything in surveying is a **measurement**, and every measurement carries error. The professional's job is not to eliminate error (impossible) but to **understand, quantify, and bound** it. This module builds that mindset in five steps:

- **Units & significant figures** — the bookkeeping that keeps answers honest. Watch the US survey foot vs international foot trap and never report more precision than you measured.
- **Error classification** — gross (blunders), systematic (one-directional, correctable), and random (the irreducible scatter statistics actually describe).
- **Statistics of a measurement set** — the most probable value (mean), residuals, and the **sample standard deviation** σ = √(Σv²/(n−1)).
- **Error propagation** — how the uncertainty in inputs flows into a sum, a series of n repeated readings, or a product such as area.
- **Probability** — the normal curve and the **68-95-99.7 rule**, weighted means, and confidence intervals.

The payoff: when the exam hands you ten distance observations, a ±tolerance on each side of a lot, or a 1:10,000 precision spec, you will know exactly which formula applies and how to key it on an NCEES-approved calculator. These are fast, high-yield points — drill them until they are reflexive.

title: Key Concepts
content:
## Accuracy vs precision **Accuracy** = closeness to the true value. **Precision** = closeness of repeated measurements to one another (repeatability). A total station can be precise (tight cluster) yet inaccurate (cluster centered on the wrong value because of an uncorrected systematic error). The classic image: tight grouping off the bullseye = precise but not accurate; scattered around the bullseye = accurate-on-average but not precise. ## The three error types
TypeCauseBehaviorTreatment
Gross (blunder/mistake)Human error: transposed digits, wrong target, misread rodLarge, sporadic, not predictableDetect & remove with redundancy/checks; never "adjust"
SystematicPhysical/instrumental: tape too long, EDM scale, refractionOne-directional, repeats in same sign/size, accumulatesCorrect by formula or procedure (e.g., temperature correction, reciprocal leveling)
Random (accidental)Irreducible limits of reading/pointingEqually likely + or −, small, follows the normal curveTreat with statistics (mean, std dev, least squares)
Only **random** error is what standard deviation and error propagation describe. Blunders must be found and thrown out first; systematic errors must be modeled/corrected first. Statistics applied to data still containing a blunder is meaningless. ## Most probable value and residuals For a set of equally-weighted direct observations, the **most probable value (MPV)** is the arithmetic mean x̄ = Σxᵢ/n. The **residual** of each observation is vᵢ = xᵢ − x̄ (observation minus the mean). Residuals are the raw material of every dispersion statistic. ## Standard deviation and standard error The **sample standard deviation** measures the scatter of a single observation about the mean: σ = √( Σv² / (n − 1) ) We divide by (n − 1), the **degrees of freedom**, not n — one degree of freedom was "used up" computing the mean. The **standard error (deviation) of the mean** measures how well the *mean itself* is known and is always smaller than σ: σ_m = σ / √n Doubling your confidence in the mean by halving σ_m requires **four times** as many observations (because of the √n). ## Error propagation When a result is computed from several measured quantities, their individual random errors **combine in quadrature** (root-sum-square), not by simple addition, because random errors partly cancel: - **Sum/difference of independent quantities:** E = √(E₁² + E₂² + … ) - **Series of n equal, independent errors** (e.g., n equal tape lengths each ±e): E = e·√n - **Product** such as area A = a·b: σ_A = √((b·σ_a)² + (a·σ_b)²) ## Probability and the normal curve Random errors follow the **normal (Gaussian) distribution**. The empirical **68-95-99.7 rule** states that about **68.3%** of observations fall within ±1σ of the mean, **95.4%** within ±2σ, and **99.7%** within ±3σ. The **probable error (E₅₀ = 0.6745σ)** is the bound containing 50% of errors. **Weights** are assigned inversely to variance, w ∝ 1/σ², so a more precise measurement (smaller σ) pulls the **weighted mean** more strongly. ![A geodetic control monument disk. Surveys are referenced to physical monuments like this one, which mark points of known horizontal and/or vertical control and carry the station designation and setting agency.](/lessons/fs/photos/geodetic-benchmark-disk.jpg "Photo: Ebyabe, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons") ![Accuracy vs. precision: a tight cluster on the bullseye is both accurate and precise; a tight cluster off-center is precise but not accurate (a systematic error); a scattered pattern centered on the bullseye is accurate on average but not precise.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/accuracy-precision.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep") ![The normal (Gaussian) distribution of random errors: about 68.3% fall within ±1σ, 95.4% within ±2σ, and 99.7% within ±3σ of the mean.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/normal-error-curve.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep") ![Traditional survey units drawn to scale: 1 foot, 1 Texas vara (2.78 ft = 33⅓ in), 1 rod (16.5 ft), and 1 Gunter's chain (66 ft = 4 rods = 100 links). 10 square chains = 1 acre.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/survey-units.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

title: Worked Examples
content:
## Example 1 — Mean, standard deviation, and standard error of the mean

![Checking a measurement by hand with a steel tape. Even in the electronic era, a good surveyor verifies distances directly in the field.](/lessons/fs/photos/starr-tape-check.jpg "Photo: Starr Surveying (field photo)")

A distance is measured 10 times (ft): 215.86, 215.80, 215.78, 215.84, 215.84, 215.83, 215.82, 215.86, 215.86, 215.81. Find the most probable value, the standard deviation, and the standard error of the mean.

**Step 1 — Mean (MPV).** Σx = 2158.30, n = 10 → x̄ = 2158.30/10 = **215.830 ft**.

**Step 2 — Residuals & Σv².** v = x − 215.830. Squaring and summing gives Σv² = 0.006600 ft².

**Step 3 — Standard deviation.**

σ = √(Σv²/(n−1)) = √(0.006600/9) = √0.0007333 = **±0.027 ft** (matches practice-exam Q6).

**Step 4 — Standard error of the mean.**

σ_m = σ/√n = 0.027/√10 = 0.027/3.1623 = **±0.0086 ft**.

**Calculator — TI-36X Pro (stat mode):** press `data`, enter all ten values in L1, `2nd [data]` (stat) → `1-Var Stats`, select L1, `calc`. Read **x̄ = 215.83** and **Sx = 0.0271** (Sx is the sample σ; the screen also shows σx, the population value — use **Sx** for n−1). Then σ_m = Sx ÷ √10.

**Calculator — Casio fx-991EX (ClassWiz):** `MENU` → `6 Statistics` → `1 (1-Variable)`, type the ten values, `AC`, then `OPTN` → `2 1-Variable Calc`. Read **x̄** and **sx** (sample std dev). HP-35S: enter values with `Σ+`, then `s` for sample std dev.

## Example 2 — Error propagation of a sum (taping a line in segments)

A line is taped in 6 equal segments; each segment's length has a random error of ±0.010 ft. What is the expected error in the total length?

**Series of n equal errors:** E = e·√n = 0.010·√6 = 0.010·2.449 = **±0.0245 ft ≈ ±0.024 ft.**

Note it is **not** 6 × 0.010 = 0.060 ft — random errors partly cancel, so they add in quadrature. Equivalently E = √(0.010² × 6).

**Calculator — TI-36X Pro:** `0.010 × √6 =` → 0.02449. (For unequal errors use √(e1²+e2²+…): square each, sum, `√`.)

## Example 3 — Error propagation of a product (area of a lot)

A rectangular lot measures 120.00 ± 0.04 ft by 144.00 ± 0.05 ft. State the area and its uncertainty.

**Area:** A = 120.00 × 144.00 = 17,280 ft².

**Propagation (product):** σ_A = √((b·σ_a)² + (a·σ_b)²) = √((144·0.04)² + (120·0.05)²) = √(5.76² + 6.00²) = √(33.18 + 36.00) = √69.18 = **±8.3 ft².**

So **A = 17,280 ± 8.3 ft²** (matches practice-exam Q2, choice B).

**Calculator — TI-36X Pro:** compute `144×0.04 = 5.76` `[STO→ x]`, `120×0.05 = 6`, then `√(5.76² + 6²)` = 8.31.

## Example 4 — Relative precision

A traverse with perimeter 2,640 ft closes with a linear misclosure of 0.22 ft. Express the relative precision.

Relative precision = misclosure / perimeter = 0.22 / 2640 = 1/12,000. **Report as 1:12,000** (always reduce numerator to 1: divide perimeter by misclosure → 2640/0.22 = 12,000).

## Example 5 — Weighted mean of redundant length measurements

A distance is measured three ways: tape 297.426 m (σ = ±0.070), EDM 297.155 m (σ = ±0.015), total-station inverse 297.209 m (σ = ±0.048). Find the most probable length.

**Step 1 — Weights ∝ 1/σ².** w_tape = 1/0.070² = 204.1; w_EDM = 1/0.015² = 4444.4; w_inv = 1/0.048² = 434.0.

**Step 2 — Weighted mean.**

x̄_w = Σ(w·x)/Σw = (204.1·297.426 + 4444.4·297.155 + 434.0·297.209) / (204.1 + 4444.4 + 434.0)
= (60,704.7 + 1,320,684.4 + 128,988.7) / 5082.5 = 1,510,377.8 / 5082.5 = **297.168 m.**

The high-precision EDM (smallest σ → largest weight) dominates, pulling the answer toward 297.155 m.

**Calculator — TI-36X Pro (weighted stat):** in stat mode use the two-column (FRQ) layout — enter values in L1 and weights in L2, run `1-Var Stats` with **FRQ = L2**; the reported x̄ is the weighted mean.

## Example 6 — The 68-95-99.7 rule

Angles are observed with σ = 4″. Within what symmetric bound do 95.4% of observations fall? That is ±2σ = ±8″. About 68.3% fall within ±4″ (±1σ); 99.7% within ±12″ (±3σ).

title: Exam Tips & Calculator Strategy
content:
## Exam strategy for this area

![A Starr Surveying crew member running a total station in the field — the everyday reality behind the theory you are studying.](/lessons/fs/photos/starr-branded-crew.jpg "Photo: Starr Surveying (field photo)")

- **These are fast points.** Stats and unit questions are usually one- or two-step. Bank them early; flag-and-skip long COGO problems. Budget ~2.9 min/question overall, but most of these take under a minute.
- **Read the n−1 vs n choice carefully.** "Standard deviation of the *set/observations*" → use sample σ (n−1). The exam's distractors almost always include the population value (÷n). On your calculator that is **Sx (TI) / sx (Casio)** for n−1 and **σx / xσn** for n.
- **Standard error of the mean has the extra √n.** If a question asks how well the *mean* is known (vs a single observation), divide by √n. Forgetting this is the #1 trap.
- **Errors add in quadrature, not linearly.** For a sum or a series, root-sum-square. If you see a clean linear sum among the choices, it is the distractor.
- **Relative precision is reported 1:N.** Divide the distance by the error and round to a "nice" denominator (1:5,000, 1:10,000…).
- **Watch the foot.** US survey foot (0.3048006096 m) vs international foot (0.3048 m exactly) differ by 2 ppm — on a state-plane coordinate that is feet of difference. The exam mixes SI and USCS; confirm units before keying.

## Approved-calculator tricks (NCEES 2026 list)

Approved: **TI-30X / TI-36X** (all), **Casio fx-115 / fx-991** (all), **HP 33s / 35s** only. No programmable/graphing/CAS models.

- **TI-36X Pro stats:** `data` to enter L1 (and L2 for frequencies/weights), `2nd [data]` → `1-Var Stats`. Read **x̄** (mean) and **Sx** (sample σ, n−1). Compute σ_m = Sx ÷ √n by hand.
- **Casio fx-991EX:** `MENU 6` Statistics → `1-Variable`; turn on the FREQ column via `SHIFT MENU (SETUP) → Statistics → Frequency On` to do weighted means. `OPTN → 1-Variable Calc` shows x̄ and **sx**.
- **HP-35S:** enter each value `Σ+`; recall **x̄** with `[x̄,ŷ]`, sample std dev with `[s]`. RPN chaining is handy but optional here.
- **Root-sum-square fast path:** `√( a x² + b x² + … )` — use the `x²` key on each term, sum, then `√`. Store an intermediate with `STO` to avoid re-keying.
- **DMS for angle-error problems:** keep the calculator in degree mode and use the `°’”` (DMS) key so angular σ values combine correctly.

## Common traps

- Applying statistics to data that still contains a **blunder** (find/remove it first) or an uncorrected **systematic** error (model it first).
- Confusing **accuracy** (closeness to truth) with **precision** (repeatability).
- Using **n** instead of **n−1** in σ.
- Adding tolerances linearly instead of in quadrature.
- Reporting more **significant figures** than the measurement justifies — carry full precision through intermediate steps, round only at the end.

## How the handbook helps

The FS Reference Handbook's **Probability and Statistics** section gives σ = √(Σv²/(n−1)), the propagation formulas (sum, series, product, mean), weighted-mean relation w ∝ 1/σ², and the **Z-value / unit-normal table** (90% → 1.6449, 95% → 1.9600). Know *where* these live so you can confirm a formula in seconds rather than deriving it. The **Conversions** section up front has every unit factor you need — bookmark both pages mentally before exam day.

title: Module Overview
content:
## Leveling — the backbone of vertical control

**Leveling** is the field operation that determines **elevations** of points relative to a **datum**. On the FS exam, leveling lives in Knowledge Area 5C (Survey Computations) with strong overlap into Area 1 (field procedures) and Area 7 (error/closure). Expect a handful of direct computational items: read a level note and find an elevation, compute a curvature-and-refraction correction, reduce a trigonometric-leveling sight, or distribute a loop misclosure.

The dominant field technique is **differential leveling** using the **height-of-instrument (HI) method**. A level set up between two points reads a **backsight (BS)** on a point of known elevation (a benchmark or turning point) and a **foresight (FS)** on the next point. Adding the BS to the known elevation gives the line-of-sight elevation, the **HI**; subtracting a FS from the HI gives the new point's elevation. Repeating this from setup to setup carries elevation across long distances.

Three relationships are non-negotiable: **HI = Elev + BS**, **Elev = HI − FS**, and the running check **ΣBS − ΣFS = Elev_last − Elev_first**. Beyond the bookkeeping you must handle systematic effects — **earth curvature and atmospheric refraction**, **instrument collimation** (line-of-sight not level, found by the **two-peg test**) — and quality control through **loop misclosure** against a known datum, then adjusting the observed elevations.

This module also covers **profile leveling** (elevations along a route for cross-sections and grades), **trigonometric leveling** (elevation from a slope distance and vertical angle), **reciprocal leveling** across obstacles, and **three-wire leveling** for higher precision. Datums you will see named: **NAVD88** (the current US vertical datum) and the older **NGVD29**; elevations are **orthometric heights (H)**, related to GPS ellipsoid heights by H = h − N.

![An automatic level set up on a tripod. Levered onto a horizontal line of sight, it reads a graduated rod for differential leveling.](/lessons/fs/photos/automatic-level.jpg "Photo: Kecko, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons")

title: Key Concepts
content:
## Datums, benchmarks, and the vertical reference A **datum** is the reference surface from which elevations are measured; in modern US practice that is the **geoid**, realized as **NAVD88**. A **benchmark (BM)** is a permanently monumented point of published, known elevation. A **turning point (TP)** is a temporary, well-defined point (e.g., a turning plate) used to transfer the line of sight from one instrument setup to the next; the rod is held on the same TP for the FS of one setup and the BS of the next. ## Backsight, foresight, and the HI method - **Backsight (BS)** — also called a **plus sight (+)**. A rod reading taken on a point of *known* elevation. **HI = Elev + BS.** - **Foresight (FS)** — also called a **minus sight (−)**. A rod reading on a point whose elevation you are *determining*. **Elev = HI − FS.** - The **HI (height of instrument)** here is the *elevation of the line of sight*, not the height of the telescope above the ground.
StationBS (+)HIFS (−)Elevation
BM-A3.21503.21500.00
TP14.05505.102.16501.05
BM-B1.74503.36
**Arithmetic check:** ΣBS = 3.21 + 4.05 = 7.26; ΣFS = 2.16 + 1.74 = 3.90; ΣBS − ΣFS = 3.36 = Elev_B − Elev_A = 503.36 − 500.00. The check confirms the *bookkeeping* (not blunders in the field). ## Curvature and refraction Over a long sight the earth curves away from the level line of sight (**curvature**, makes rod readings read **too high**), and the line of sight bends downward through the atmosphere (**refraction**, partly offsetting curvature). Net, for rod readings in feet with the sight distance **F expressed in thousands of feet**: - Curvature only: **C = 0.0240·F²** ft - Combined curvature & refraction: **C_R = 0.0206·F²** ft Balancing BS and FS distances **cancels** curvature & refraction in differential leveling — a key reason to keep sight distances equal. ## Collimation error and the two-peg test **Collimation error** is a line of sight that is not truly horizontal when the bubble is centered. The **two-peg test** detects it: set two pegs A and B a known distance apart; from the midpoint, equal sight distances cancel any collimation and give the *true* ΔElev; then set up near one peg (unequal distances) and re-read — the discrepancy is the collimation error per unit of distance difference. In differential leveling the residual collimation effect is **(collimation rate)·(ΣBS dist − ΣFS dist)**, again zeroed by balancing sights. ## Trigonometric leveling When a slope distance **S** (or horizontal distance **d**) and a **vertical angle V** (above horizontal) are measured, the elevation difference is **ΔElev = S·sin V = d·tan V**, adjusted for instrument height (hi) and rod/target height (hr): ΔElev = S·sin V + hi − hr. For long sights add the C_R correction. (Note: if a **zenith angle z** is measured instead, ΔElev = S·cos z.) ## Loop misclosure and adjustment A level **loop** returns to a benchmark of known elevation (or closes back on the start). The **misclosure** = observed (ΣBS − ΣFS) minus the known elevation difference. If within tolerance, distribute the correction in proportion to **distance leveled** (or number of setups). Federal/typical order-of-accuracy tolerances scale with √(distance): e.g., third-order ≈ 0.05·√(miles) ft. **Reciprocal leveling** (reading both ends from each bank) cancels curvature/refraction and collimation across rivers/canyons; **three-wire leveling** averages upper/middle/lower crosshair readings for precision and a built-in check. ![Differential leveling: a backsight (BS) on a benchmark establishes the Height of Instrument (HI = Elev + BS); a foresight (FS) on the turning point gives its elevation (Elev = HI − FS).](/lessons/fs/diagrams/differential-leveling.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep") ![Curvature and refraction on a level sight: the earth curves away from the horizontal line of sight (making a distant reading too high), while atmospheric refraction bends the ray back down by about one-seventh; the net effect is c − r ≈ 0.0206·F² ft (F in thousands of feet).](/lessons/fs/diagrams/curvature-refraction.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

title: Essential Formulas
content:
## Differential leveling (HI method)

- **Height of instrument:** HI = Elev_BM + BS
- **Point elevation:** Elev = HI − FS
- **Net elevation change (multi-setup):** ΔElev = ΣBS − ΣFS
- **Arithmetic (page) check:** Elev_last − Elev_first = ΣBS − ΣFS

## Curvature & refraction (rod readings, USCS)

With sight distance **F in thousands of feet**:

- Curvature only: **C = 0.0240·F²** ft
- Curvature + refraction: **C_R = 0.0206·F²** ft
- (Metric, K in km: C = 0.0785·K² m; C_R = 0.0675·K² m)
- Vertical-angle form (handbook): c ≈ 4.905″/1000 ft; (c & r) ≈ 4.244″/1000 ft

## Trigonometric leveling

- **ΔElev = S·sin(V) = d·tan(V)**  (V = vertical angle above horizontal)
- With instrument/rod heights: **ΔElev = S·sin(V) + hi − hr**
- Zenith-angle form: ΔElev = S·cos(z)
- New elevation: Elev_B = Elev_A + ΔElev

## Loop / line misclosure & adjustment

- **Misclosure** = (ΣBS − ΣFS)_observed − (Elev_known_end − Elev_known_start)
- **Correction at a point** = −Misclosure × (distance to point / total distance)
- Closure tolerance (typical 3rd order): allowable = 0.05·√(M) ft, M = miles leveled

## Reciprocal & three-wire leveling

- **Reciprocal Δh:** Δh = ½[(a₁ − b₁) + (a₂ − b₂)]
- **Three-wire mean reading:** R = (Upper + Middle + Lower)/3; half-interval check: (U − M) ≈ (M − L)
- **Stadia interval → distance:** D ≈ 100·(U − L)

## Collimation

- **Collimation correction:** ΔC = e·(ΣBS dist − ΣFS dist), where e = collimation rate (ft of error per ft of sight, e.g., 0.012/100)

## Orthometric vs ellipsoid height

- **H = h − N** (H orthometric/leveled elevation, h GPS ellipsoid height, N geoid height)

Note balancing BS = FS distances cancels this entirely. ## Example 4 — Trigonometric leveling **Given:** From station A (Elev 500.00 ft) a total station measures to a prism at B: horizontal distance **d = 620.0 ft**, vertical angle **V = +3°45′00″** above horizontal, instrument height hi = 5.30 ft, prism height hr = 5.30 ft (equal). **Solve:** 1. Convert angle: 3°45′ = 3.75°. `3` `°’”` `45` `°’”` `=` on TI-36X gives 3.75°. 2. ΔElev = d·tan(V) = 620.0 × tan(3.75°) = 620.0 × 0.065543 = **40.64 ft** 3. Add hi − hr = 0, so Elev_B = 500.00 + 40.64 = **540.64 ft** **Check with slope form:** S = d/cos V = 620.0/0.99786 = 621.3 ft; ΔElev = S·sin V = 621.3 × 0.065399 = 40.63 ft ✓ (rounding). **Calculator:** put the calculator in DEG mode; for a zenith angle z use `S × cos(z)` instead. ## Example 5 — Loop misclosure & adjustment **Given:** A level loop starts on BM-100 (Elev 250.000 ft) and is run through field points back to **BM-101 (published Elev 263.420 ft)**. The notes give ΣBS = 41.275 ft and ΣFS = 27.810 ft over **0.80 miles**. **Solve:** 1. Observed ΔElev = ΣBS − ΣFS = 41.275 − 27.810 = **13.465 ft** → observed Elev_BM-101 = 250.000 + 13.465 = 263.465 ft 2. Misclosure = observed − known = 263.465 − 263.420 = **+0.045 ft** 3. Allowable (3rd order) = 0.05·√0.80 = 0.05 × 0.894 = 0.045 ft → **just within tolerance** 4. Distribute −0.045 ft across the run in proportion to distance; the corrected closing elevation becomes the published **263.420 ft**. **Calculator:** `0.05 × 0.80 √ =` for the tolerance; sign of the misclosure tells you which way to push the elevations.

title: Exam Tips & Calculator Strategy
content:
## Strategy for leveling items

- **Memorize the three core relations** so you never look them up: **HI = Elev + BS**, **Elev = HI − FS**, **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΔElev**. These solve the majority of leveling questions in seconds.
- **BS is always a plus, FS is always a minus.** The single most common trap is swapping them. Write a tiny two-column BS/FS table in the margin even for a one-setup problem.
- **Always run the arithmetic check** (ΣBS − ΣFS = last − first). If it fails, you mis-added a column — fix it before trusting the elevation.
- **Watch the units of F in curvature & refraction.** The handbook constants 0.0240 and 0.0206 assume **F in *thousands* of feet**. A 3,000-ft sight is F = 3, not 3000. Forgetting this inflates the answer by 10⁶.
- **Curvature reads the rod too HIGH; refraction lowers the apparent reading.** Net C_R = 0.0206·F² is *subtracted* from a long FS. Balancing BS and FS distances cancels both — a frequent "why do we keep sights equal?" concept question.
- **Trig leveling:** confirm whether the angle is a **vertical angle** (from horizontal → use sin/tan) or a **zenith angle** (from vertical → use cos). Add hi, subtract hr. Put the calculator in **DEG** mode.
- **Misclosure sign:** misclosure = observed − known. Corrections have the *opposite* sign and are spread by **distance or setup count**.

## Approved-calculator tricks (TI-36X Pro / Casio fx-991 / HP 33s-35s)

- **DMS entry:** TI-36X Pro — type the degrees, `°’”`, minutes, `°’”`, seconds, `°’”`, then `=`; Casio fx-991 uses the `°’”` key the same way. This converts 3°45′ to 3.75° for the tan() call. HP 35s: enter `3.4500` then `→HR`.
- **Chaining a level run:** store ΣBS in memory A and ΣFS in memory B as you add the columns, then `RCL A − RCL B` for ΔElev — avoids re-keying.
- **C_R fast path:** `(F) x² × 0.0206 =`. Keep F in thousands of feet.
- **Reciprocal leveling:** compute Δh = ½[(a₁−b₁)+(a₂−b₂)] directly; the averaging cancels curvature/refraction and collimation.
- **Three-wire:** mean = (U+M+L)/3 and check that (U−M) ≈ (M−L); distance ≈ 100·(U−L).

## How the FS Reference Handbook helps

- The handbook's **Curvature and refraction** block gives the 0.0240/0.0206 (ft) and 0.0785/0.0675 (m) constants plus the arc-second forms — search "curvature" rather than re-deriving.
- Leveling bookkeeping (HI, BS, FS) is **not** a boxed formula; you must know it cold. The handbook only supplies the constants and the trig.
- For trig leveling, use the handbook's **trigonometry / right-triangle** relations; for tolerances, leveling closure follows the supplied **FGCS Geodetic Leveling** standard logic (allowable ∝ √distance).

title: Module Overview
content:
## Field Data Acquisition: Distances and Angles

Every coordinate, traverse, and boundary computation on the FS exam ultimately rests on two raw field observations: a **distance** and a **direction (angle)**. This module covers how those observations are actually made and, more importantly for the exam, how they are **corrected and reduced** into the clean numbers you later feed into COGO.

You will work through three eras of distance measurement that the exam still tests:

1. **Taping (chaining)** — and its five systematic corrections: temperature, tension/pull, sag, slope, and standardization. The exam loves a tape-correction problem because it isolates one concept and rewards careful sign handling.
2. **EDM (electronic distance measurement)** — the phase/pulse principle, the **instrument (additive) constant**, and the **atmospheric ppm** correction tied to temperature and pressure.
3. **Total stations** — which marry an EDM to an electronic theodolite, plus robotic and reflectorless variants.

On the angular side you will master **horizontal angles, vertical angles, and zenith angles**, the **direct-and-reverse** (face-left/face-right) procedure that cancels instrumental error, and the conversions that trip up examinees under time pressure: **DMS↔decimal degrees**, **azimuth↔bearing**, **back-azimuth**, and the **magnetic declination** correction for historical (record) bearings.

Finally you will reduce a **slope distance to a horizontal distance** using the zenith angle — the single most common reduction in trigonometric field work: **H = S·sin(Z)**.

Because the NCEES calculator (TI-36X Pro / Casio fx-991) does DMS entry, DMS arithmetic, and rectangular↔polar conversion natively, this module pairs every worked example with the exact keystrokes so the conversions become reflexive on exam day.

![A modern total station. It combines an electronic theodolite (angle measurement) with an EDM (electronic distance measurement) to capture horizontal and vertical angles plus slope distance in one setup.](/lessons/fs/photos/total-station.jpg "Photo: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons")

title: Key Concepts
content:
## 1. Taping and its corrections

A steel tape is standardized (calibrated) at a known **temperature (68°F / 20°C)**, a known **tension (pull)**, and a known **support condition** (fully supported on a flat surface, or supported only at the ends). When field conditions differ, the measured length is systematically wrong and must be corrected. The five standard corrections:

![A surveyor sighting through an optical theodolite. The theodolite measures horizontal and vertical angles — the angular half of every distance-and-angle observation.](/lessons/fs/photos/m3-theodolite.jpg "Photo: Queensland State Archives — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons")

- **Temperature** — steel expands when warm. `Ct = α·(T − Ts)·L` with the coefficient of thermal expansion for steel **α = 0.00000645 / °F** (i.e. 6.45×10⁻⁶ per °F) and standard temperature **Ts = 68°F**. Hot tape reads short (so the correction is positive when T > 68°F for a measured distance).
- **Tension / pull** — pulling harder than standard stretches the tape: `Cp = (P − P0)·L / (A·E)`, where A = cross-sectional area, E = modulus of elasticity (≈29,000,000 psi for steel).
- **Sag** — an unsupported tape hangs in a catenary and reads **long**, so the correction is always **negative**: `Cs = −w²·L³ / (24·P²)`, w = weight per foot, P = applied tension.
- **Slope** — a tape stretched along a slope measures the slope distance, not the horizontal. The reduction `Ch ≈ −h²/(2L)` (h = elevation difference) or exactly `H = S·cos(vertical angle)`.
- **Standardization** — the tape's true length differs from its nominal length (e.g. a "100 ft" tape is actually 100.012 ft). Add the per-tape-length error proportionally.

**Sign discipline is everything.** Decide whether you are (a) *measuring a distance in the field* or (b) *laying out a distance to set a point* — the sign of every correction flips between the two cases.

## 2. EDM and total stations

An **EDM** transmits a modulated light/IR wave to a prism (or directly to a surface, *reflectorless*) and infers distance from the phase shift (or pulse time-of-flight). Two errors dominate exam problems:

- **Instrument (additive/zero) constant** — a fixed offset `a` in mm, independent of distance.
- **Scale / ppm error** — proportional to distance, expressed in **parts per million**. Atmospheric conditions matter: roughly a **10°C** temperature change **or** a **1 in Hg (≈25 mm Hg)** pressure change is about **10 ppm**. Total stated EDM precision is written as **±(a mm + b ppm)**.

A **total station** combines an EDM with an electronic (digital) theodolite and an onboard processor, outputting horizontal angle, zenith angle, and slope distance — and computing H, V, and coordinates internally. **Robotic** total stations track a prism for one-person crews; **reflectorless** units measure to a surface without a prism.

## 3. Angles: horizontal, vertical, zenith

- **Horizontal angle** — measured in the horizontal plane between two directions; the basis of traverse turning angles and angles-to-the-right.
- **Vertical angle (α)** — measured **up (+) or down (−) from the horizontal** (0° = level).
- **Zenith angle (Z)** — measured **down from the upward vertical** (zenith). A level sight = **90°**. Relationship: **Z = 90° − α**. Most modern total stations read **zenith** angles.

## 4. Direct and reverse (D&R)

Observing an angle in both telescope positions — **direct (face left / face I)** and **reverse (face right / face II, telescope plunged)** — and **meaning** the two cancels instrumental errors (collimation, horizontal-axis tilt, vertical-circle index). The mean of D&R is the accepted angle; the **2C** (direct + reverse − 360°) checks collimation.

## 5. Directions: azimuths, bearings, declination

- **Azimuth** — clockwise angle from a reference meridian (usually north), **0°–360°**.
- **Bearing** — acute angle (0°–90°) from north OR south, toward east or west, written as a quadrant call (e.g. **N42°15′E**, **S08°40′W**).
- **Back-azimuth** = Az ± 180° (use + if Az < 180°, − if Az ≥ 180°). **Back-bearing** = same angle, opposite quadrant letters.
- **Magnetic declination** — the angle between magnetic north and true (geodetic) north at a place and date. **East declination is added** to a magnetic bearing to get true; **west declination is subtracted**. Converting old magnetic deed calls to true direction (and accounting for *secular change* in declination between two dates) is a classic boundary/retracement question.

![Bearings versus azimuths. Azimuths run clockwise from North (0°–360°); bearings are measured ≤ 90° from N or S toward E or W. The quadrant fixes the conversion.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/bearings-azimuths.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![Reducing a slope distance to horizontal: for slope distance S at vertical angle α, the horizontal distance is H = S·cos α and the vertical difference is V = S·sin α.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/slope-reduction.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![Measuring a horizontal angle: the instrument occupies station B, sights the backsight A, then the foresight C; the clockwise angle A→C is the measured angle. Averaging a direct and a reversed (plunged) reading cancels instrument errors.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/angle-measurement.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![Height of an inaccessible point from two setups: sighting the top from two stations a known distance apart (angles A and B) gives h = d / (cot A − cot B).](/lessons/fs/diagrams/tower-two-angles.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep (generated)")

title: Essential Formulas
content:
## Taping corrections (apply to a measured length L)

**Temperature (thermal):**

`Ct = 0.00000645 · (T − 68) · L`   (L, Ct in ft; T in °F; α_steel = 6.45×10⁻⁶/°F)

Metric form: `Ct = 0.0000116 · (T − 20) · L` (T in °C, α = 11.6×10⁻⁶/°C).

**Tension / pull:**

`Cp = (P − P0)·L / (A·E)`   (P, P0 in lb; A in in²; E ≈ 29,000,000 psi for steel)

**Sag (always negative — tape reads long):**

`Cs = − w²·L³ / (24·P²)`   (w = weight per ft; or `Cs = −W²·L/(24·P²)` with total weight W)

**Slope reduction (slope length S → horizontal H):**

`H = S · cos(α)`   (α = vertical angle)  •  `H = S · sin(Z)`   (Z = zenith angle)

Approximate correction: `Ch ≈ − h² / (2L)`   (h = elevation difference over length L)

**Standardization:** `Cstd = (actual tape length − nominal) · (measured / nominal)`

**Corrected length:** `L_corrected = L_measured + Ct + Cp + Cs + Ch + Cstd`

## EDM

**Combined stated error / correction:**

`e(mm) = a_mm + b_ppm · D_km · 1000`   ⇒ for D in km, ppm term in mm = `b · D_km`

Equivalently, for D in meters: `e(mm) = a + b·(D/1,000,000)·... ` — simplest: ppm error (mm) = `b · D(km)`.

Atmospheric rule of thumb: ≈ **10 ppm per 10°C** or per **1 in Hg** pressure difference.

## Angles

`Z = 90° − α`   (zenith ↔ vertical angle)

`2C = (Direct + Reverse) − 360°`   (collimation check; mean angle = (D + (R−180°))/2)

## DMS ↔ decimal degrees

`dd = D + M/60 + S/3600`

`D = trunc(dd)` ; `M = trunc((dd − D)·60)` ; `S = (((dd − D)·60) − M)·60`

Total seconds: `total" = D·3600 + M·60 + S`

## Azimuth ↔ bearing (by quadrant of the azimuth)

| Quadrant | Azimuth range | Bearing | Az→Brg | Brg→Az |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I — NE | 0°–90° | N (Az) E | brg = Az | Az = brg |
| II — SE | 90°–180° | S (180−Az) E | brg = 180 − Az | Az = 180 − brg |
| III — SW | 180°–270° | S (Az−180) W | brg = Az − 180 | Az = 180 + brg |
| IV — NW | 270°–360° | N (360−Az) W | brg = 360 − Az | Az = 360 − brg |

**Back-azimuth:** `Back-Az = Az + 180°` (if Az < 180°) or `Az − 180°` (if Az ≥ 180°).

## Magnetic declination

`True = Magnetic + East_declination`  •  `True = Magnetic − West_declination`

Secular change between dates: apply the *difference* in declination to convert an old magnetic call to a present-day true (or current magnetic) direction.

title: Worked Examples
content:
## Example 1 — Temperature tape correction

![A retroreflective prism target. A total station’s EDM fires an infrared beam at the prism and times its return to measure slope distance to the point.](/lessons/fs/photos/m3-prism-pole.jpg "Photo: KJG2007 — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons")

A line is measured with a steel tape standardized at 68°F as **measured length = 842.60 ft**. The field temperature was **96°F**. What is the corrected horizontal length (tape fully supported, standard tension)?

**Solution.** Use `Ct = 0.00000645·(T − 68)·L`:

`Ct = 0.00000645 × (96 − 68) × 842.60 = 0.00000645 × 28 × 842.60 = +0.152 ft`

The tape was hot, so it read short; the true distance is longer:

`L_corrected = 842.60 + 0.152 = 842.75 ft`

**TI-36X Pro keystrokes:** `0.00000645 × ( 96 − 68 ) × 842.60 =` → 0.15225. Then `842.60 + 0.15225 =`. (Enter 6.45E-6 with the `×10ⁿ` / `EE` key: `6.45` `×10ⁿ` `(-) 6`.)

**Casio fx-991:** identical; use the `×10ˣ` key for the exponent: `6.45` `×10ˣ` `(−)6`.

---

## Example 2 — Slope distance → horizontal distance (zenith angle)

A total station reads a **slope distance S = 415.270 ft** to a prism with a **zenith angle Z = 87°12′30″**. What is the horizontal distance?

**Solution.** `H = S · sin(Z)`. First get Z into the calculator in DMS:

Enter `87°12′30″` using the DMS key, then `H = 415.270 × sin(Z)`.

`sin(87°12′30″) = sin(87.20833°) = 0.998813`

`H = 415.270 × 0.998813 = 414.777 ft`

**TI-36X Pro keystrokes:** put calc in **DEG** mode. `415.270 × sin( 87 [°’”] 12 [°’”] 30 [°’”] ) =` → 414.777. The `[°’”]` key is `2nd` `[matrix/angle]` → `°’”` (the DMS template). You may also type 87 `°’”` 12 `°’”` 30 `°’”`.

**Casio fx-991:** `415.270 × sin( 87 [°’’’] 12 [°’’’] 30 [°’’’] ) =`. The `°’’’` key enters and displays sexagesimal directly; pressing `=` then `°’’’` toggles a result between decimal and DMS.

*Check with the vertical angle:* α = 90° − 87°12′30″ = 2°47′30″, and `H = S·cos(α) = 415.270 × cos(2.79167°) = 414.777 ft`. ✓

---

## Example 3 — DMS arithmetic and DMS↔decimal

**(a)** Convert **218°43′52″** to decimal degrees.

`dd = 218 + 43/60 + 52/3600 = 218 + 0.716667 + 0.014444 = 218.731111°`

**(b)** Add two angles: **47°38′45″ + 22°51′30″**.

Seconds: 45 + 30 = 75″ → 1′15″. Minutes: 38 + 51 + 1 = 90′ → 1°30′. Degrees: 47 + 22 + 1 = 70°. Result = **70°30′15″**.

**TI-36X Pro:** `47 °’” 38 °’” 45 °’” + 22 °’” 51 °’” 30 °’” =` displays **70°30′15″** directly (the calculator carries the base-60 arithmetic). Press `2nd` `[°’”]` (the `▸DMS`/`▸DD` toggle) to flip the answer to decimal.

**Casio fx-991:** `47°’’’38°’’’45°’’’ + 22°’’’51°’’’30°’’’ =` → `70°30′15″`. Press `°’’’` again to read 70.50416667°.

---

## Example 4 — Azimuth ↔ bearing and back-azimuth

A line has **azimuth 218°43′52″**. Find its bearing and its back-azimuth.

**Bearing:** azimuth is in **Quadrant III (180°–270°, SW)**, so `bearing = Az − 180° = 218°43′52″ − 180° = 38°43′52″`, written **S 38°43′52″ W**.

**Back-azimuth:** Az ≥ 180°, so `Back-Az = 218°43′52″ − 180° = 38°43′52″`.

*(Sanity check: the back-azimuth's bearing is N 38°43′52″ E — the exact reverse quadrant of S 38°43′52″ W. ✓)*

---

## Example 5 — EDM constant + ppm error

An EDM is rated **±(2 mm + 2 ppm)**. For a measured distance **D = 1,850 m**, what is the worst-case standard error in mm?

**Solution.** ppm term = `b · D(km) = 2 × 1.850 = 3.70 mm`. Constant term = 2 mm.

`e = a + b·D(km) = 2 + 2(1.850) = 2 + 3.70 = 5.70 mm`

So the line is good to about **±5.7 mm** (≈ ±0.006 m).

**Calculator:** trivial — `2 + 2 × 1.850 =`. The trap is unit handling: convert D to **km** before multiplying by the ppm figure (2 ppm of 1,850,000 mm = 3.7 mm).

---

## Example 6 — Magnetic declination (retracement)

An 1885 deed calls a line **N 12°30′ E (magnetic)**. The magnetic declination at that place and date was **8°15′ East**. What is the **true** bearing of the line?

**Solution.** East declination is **added** to a magnetic bearing measured toward the east:

`True = N (12°30′ + 8°15′) E = N 20°45′ E`

If you then needed to re-run the line today with a compass, you would apply the *present-day* declination (and its sign) instead, accounting for secular change.

This one is pure arithmetic, which means it works on every approved calculator. Follow it through.

title: Exam Tips & Calculator Strategy
content:
## Exam strategy for distance & angle items

![Sighting through the total station to turn a precise angle — steady setup, careful pointing, and a check angle are what keep angular error small.](/lessons/fs/photos/starr-total-station-sighting.jpg "Photo: Starr Surveying (field photo)")

- **Read for the reduction asked.** Many problems give a slope distance and a zenith angle and ask for *horizontal distance* — that is just `H = S·sin(Z)`. Don't over-build it.
- **Sign of every correction.** Decide first: am I *measuring* (correcting a field reading) or *laying out* (setting a point)? Sag is **always negative**; temperature follows the sign of (T − 68); slope reduction always *shortens* slope to horizontal.
- **Zenith vs vertical angle.** A level sight is **Z = 90°** and **α = 0°**. If a problem gives a "vertical angle" near 0° use `cos`; if it gives a "zenith angle" near 90° use `sin`. Mixing them is the #1 trap. `Z = 90° − α`.
- **EDM ppm needs km.** Convert the distance to kilometers before multiplying by the ppm rating (2 ppm × 1.85 km = 3.7 mm). 10 ppm ≈ 10°C or 1 in Hg of atmosphere.
- **Quadrant before conversion.** For azimuth↔bearing, identify the quadrant from the azimuth first, then apply the matching rule (NE: same; SE: 180−; SW: −180; NW: 360−). Back-azimuth is ±180°.
- **Declination direction.** "East is least, west is best" is backwards for *magnetic→true*: for a true-from-magnetic conversion, **add east declination, subtract west**. Watch whether the problem wants magnetic→true or true→magnetic (the sign flips).

## Approved-calculator tricks (TI-36X Pro / Casio fx-991)

- **DMS entry & arithmetic:** Use the **°’”** (TI) / **°’’’** (Casio) key to enter angles directly as D°M'S". The calculator does base-60 add/subtract/multiply for you — never convert to decimal by hand on the exam unless asked. Toggle a result between DMS and decimal with `2nd °’”` (TI) or by pressing `°’’’` again (Casio).
- **DEG mode:** confirm the calculator is in **degrees** (not RAD/GRAD) before any trig — a wrong angle mode silently corrupts every answer.
- **R▸P / P▸R (rectangular↔polar):** for inverse-type and forward-coordinate work, `R▸P` converts (ΔE, ΔN) → (distance, azimuth) in one step, and `P▸R` converts (distance, azimuth) → (ΔE, ΔN). On the TI-36X Pro these live under `2nd` `[R▸P]`/`[P▸R]`; on the Casio fx-991 use `Pol(` and `Rec(`. This is the fastest path for slope/azimuth bookkeeping and carries straight into the next module's COGO.
- **HP-33S/35S (RPN, if used):** `→POL`/`→REC` and `→HMS`/`→HR` give the same conversions; enter DMS as `D.MMSSss` and use `→HR` to decimalize.
- **Store-and-recall:** stash a standardized-tape length or a declination value in memory so you don't re-key it across a multi-part problem.

## How the handbook helps

The NCEES FS Reference Handbook gives you the EDM relationship (V = c/n, λ = V/f), the curvature-&-refraction constants, the azimuth/bearing quadrant constants (C = 0/180/180/360), and the inverse/forward direction formulas verbatim. Know *where* taping corrections and the slope reduction live so you can confirm a coefficient under time pressure instead of trusting memory. Practice every conversion on the actual handbook PDF before exam day.

title: Module Overview
content:
## Why this module is the heart of the FS exam

**Survey Computations and Computer Applications** is one of the two largest computational areas on the NCEES FS exam (17–26 of 110 questions), and **traversing and coordinate geometry (COGO) sit at its center**. Nearly every applied surveying problem — boundary, control, construction, topographic, route — eventually reduces to the same handful of operations you will drill here: turn a **bearing and distance** into a **latitude and departure**, accumulate them into **coordinates**, check the **closure**, **adjust** the traverse, and compute **area**.

A **traverse** is a series of connected lines (courses) whose lengths and directions are measured, used to establish horizontal control and to locate boundaries. The three families are:

- **Open traverse** — starts at a known point but ends at an unknown point; no closure check possible (avoid for control).
- **Closed-loop (polygon) traverse** — returns to its starting point; the latitudes must sum to zero and the departures must sum to zero, giving a closure check.
- **Closed-connecting (link) traverse** — starts and ends on two *different* known control points; closure is checked against the known coordinate difference.

The **two reciprocal operations** you must perform reflexively on the calculator are the **forward computation** (azimuth + distance → ΔN, ΔE → new coordinates, done with **polar→rectangular, P▸R**) and the **inverse** (two coordinates → distance + azimuth, done with **rectangular→polar, R▸P**). Master these two, plus the **shoelace** area formula, and you can solve the majority of the computational items on the exam.

This module assumes Module 3 (angles, bearings, azimuths, and DMS arithmetic). Here we put those directions to work building and adjusting traverses and computing coordinates and areas. **Every formula matches the NCEES FS Reference Handbook v2.5** so the on-screen exam reference will look familiar.

![Running a traverse in the field: the instrument occupies each station in turn, measuring the angle and distance to the next, and those observations are reduced to coordinates by latitudes and departures.](/lessons/fs/photos/field-surveyor.jpg "Photo: Random Guy of the Century, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons")

title: Key Concepts
content:
## Latitude and departure

Every course has a **length L** and a **direction** (azimuth Az measured clockwise from north, or a quadrant bearing). Resolve the course onto the coordinate axes:

![A total station set up over a control point during a traverse. Each setup measures the angle and distance to the next station, and coordinates are propagated by latitudes and departures.](/lessons/fs/photos/m4-total-station-road.jpg "Photo: FBenjr123 — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons")

- **Latitude** = the north–south component = the change in **Northing**: `Lat = ΔN = L·cos(Az)`
- **Departure** = the east–west component = the change in **Easting**: `Dep = ΔE = L·sin(Az)`

**Sign convention is automatic when you use azimuth** (0°–360°): cos and sin already deliver the correct signs. North latitudes are +, south −; east departures +, west −. If you work with quadrant bearings, apply the sign by quadrant (N+/S−, E+/W−).

## Building coordinates (the forward computation)

Starting from a known point (N₁, E₁), the next point is:

`N₂ = N₁ + L·cos(Az)`   `E₂ = E₁ + L·sin(Az)`

Walk the traverse course by course, accumulating coordinates. On the calculator this is **polar→rectangular (P▸R)**: enter (L, Az) and read back (ΔN, ΔE) — note the surveying convention puts the **angle from north**, so the *x*-result is the departure and the *y*-result is the latitude.

## Closure of a traverse

For a **closed-loop** traverse the course components must close on themselves: ideally **ΣLat = 0** and **ΣDep = 0**. Measurement error makes them small nonzero values — the **closure in latitude** (`C_N = ΣLat`) and **closure in departure** (`C_E = ΣDep`). Combine them into the **linear misclosure**:

`e = √((ΣLat)² + (ΣDep)²)`

The quality of the work is the **relative precision** (precision ratio):

`RP = perimeter / e`, reported as **1:RP** (e.g., 1:12,000). Higher is better; boundary and control work commonly require 1:5,000 to 1:10,000 or better.

## Traverse adjustment

If the misclosure is acceptable, distribute it to force the traverse to close:

- **Compass (Bowditch) rule** — the most common. The correction to each course's latitude/departure is proportional to that course's **length** relative to the perimeter:
  - `C_lat,i = −(ΣLat)·(Lᵢ / P)`   `C_dep,i = −(ΣDep)·(Lᵢ / P)`
  - Assumes angles and distances are of comparable precision (typical of total-station work).
- **Transit rule** — the correction is proportional to the **magnitude of the latitude (or departure)** of the course rather than its length:
  - `C_lat,i = −(ΣLat)·(|Latᵢ| / Σ|Lat|)`   `C_dep,i = −(ΣDep)·(|Depᵢ| / Σ|Dep|)`
  - Used (historically) when angles are more precise than distances.
- **Least squares** — the rigorous method (Module on adjustments); compass/transit are the hand methods the FS tests.

After adjustment, the corrected latitudes sum to zero and corrected departures sum to zero, so the adjusted coordinates close.

## The inverse problem

Given two coordinates, recover the **distance and direction** between them:

- `ΔN = N₂ − N₁`, `ΔE = E₂ − E₁`
- **Distance** `D = √(ΔN² + ΔE²)`
- **Azimuth** `Az = atan2(ΔE, ΔN)` normalized to 0°–360° (or `Az = arctan(ΔE/ΔN) + C`, with the handbook quadrant constant C: 0° in NE, 180° in SE and SW, 360° in NW).

On the calculator this is **rectangular→polar (R▸P)**: enter (ΔE, ΔN), read distance and angle.

## Intersections

- **Bearing–bearing**: two lines of known direction from two known points; solve the two `(E − E₀) = (N − N₀)·tan(Az)` equations for the common point.
- **Bearing–distance**: a direction from one point and a radius (distance) from another (one or two solutions).
- **Distance–distance**: two radii (circle–circle); two possible intersection points.

## Area by coordinates (shoelace)

Once every corner has coordinates, the enclosed area is, for points numbered in order around the polygon:

`A = ½·|Σ Xᵢ(Y_{i+1} − Y_{i−1})|`

equivalently `A = ½·|Σ (Xᵢ·Y_{i+1} − X_{i+1}·Yᵢ)|`. Divide ft² by **43,560** to get acres. This is the modern replacement for the legacy **DMD (double meridian distance)** method, which is still occasionally tested but gives the same result.

![Latitude and departure are the N–S and E–W components of a traverse leg: Latitude = D·cos(Az), Departure = D·sin(Az). A closed traverse must sum to ΣLat = 0 and ΣDep = 0.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/latitude-departure.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![A closed-loop traverse A→B→C→D→A: each course is measured by bearing and distance; latitudes and departures should sum to zero, and the small leftover is the linear misclosure, distributed by the compass (Bowditch) rule.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/closed-traverse.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

title: Essential Formulas
content:
## Components of a course

| Quantity | Formula | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Latitude (ΔN) | `Lat = L·cos(Az)` | + north, − south (automatic with azimuth) |
| Departure (ΔE) | `Dep = L·sin(Az)` | + east, − west (automatic with azimuth) |
| Course length (from components) | `L = √(Lat² + Dep²)` | the inverse distance |
| Course azimuth (from components) | `Az = atan2(Dep, Lat)`, normalize 0–360° | quadrant from signs of Lat, Dep |

## Forward (coordinates of a new point)

`N₂ = N₁ + L·cos(Az)`     `E₂ = E₁ + L·sin(Az)`

## Closure and precision (closed-loop)

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Closure in latitude | `C_N = ΣLat` |
| Closure in departure | `C_E = ΣDep` |
| Linear misclosure | `e = √((ΣLat)² + (ΣDep)²)` |
| Relative precision | `RP = P / e` → report **1:RP** |
| Azimuth of misclosure | `Az_e = atan2(−ΣDep, −ΣLat)` |

(P = perimeter = ΣL.)

## Compass (Bowditch) rule

`C_lat,i = −C_N·(Lᵢ / P)`     `C_dep,i = −C_E·(Lᵢ / P)`

Adjusted latitude = `Latᵢ + C_lat,i`; adjusted departure = `Depᵢ + C_dep,i`.

## Transit rule

`C_lat,i = −C_N·(|Latᵢ| / Σ|Lat|)`     `C_dep,i = −C_E·(|Depᵢ| / Σ|Dep|)`

## Inverse (rectangular → polar)

`ΔN = N₂ − N₁`,  `ΔE = E₂ − E₁`

`D = √(ΔN² + ΔE²) = hypot(ΔN, ΔE)`

`Az = atan2(ΔE, ΔN)`, then add 360° if negative → 0°–360°.

Handbook quadrant form: `θ = arctan(ΔE/ΔN) + C`, with **C = 0° (NE), 180° (SE), 180° (SW), 360° (NW)**.

## Bearing ↔ azimuth

| Quadrant | Bearing → Azimuth | Azimuth → Bearing |
|---|---|---|
| NE | Az = β | β = Az |
| SE | Az = 180° − β | β = 180° − Az |
| SW | Az = 180° + β | β = Az − 180° |
| NW | Az = 360° − β | β = 360° − Az |

**Back-azimuth** = Az ± 180°.

## Area by coordinates (shoelace)

`A = ½·|Σ (Xᵢ·Y_{i+1} − X_{i+1}·Yᵢ)|`   (close the polygon: last point connects to first)

Acres = A(ft²) / 43,560.

## A labeled 4-leg closed traverse

![A handheld EDM / data collector. Modern traverse and COGO work is recorded and reduced electronically in the field, but the underlying geometry is exactly what you compute by hand here.](/lessons/fs/photos/m4-data-collector.jpg "Photo: Krzysztof Maria Różański, ( Upior polnocy ) — CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons")

The traverse **A → B → C → D → A** below is computed throughout these examples. Bearings/azimuths and distances are labeled on each leg.

  <!-- leg labels -->
  <text x="190" y="320" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">A→B: N 90°00′ E (Az 90°), 600.00 ft</text>
  <text x="372" y="210" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">B→C: N 14°02′ W</text>
  <text x="372" y="226" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">(Az 345°57′47″), 412.31 ft</text>
  <text x="150" y="230" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">C→D: S 81°28′ W</text>
  <text x="150" y="246" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">(Az 261°28′, 273.0 ft)</text>
  <text x="50" y="230" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">D→A:</text>
  <text x="30" y="246" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">S 18°26′ E,</text>
  <text x="30" y="262" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">158.1 ft</text>
</svg>

For clean arithmetic we use these legs (azimuths from north):

| Leg | Azimuth | Distance L (ft) |
|---|---|---|
| A→B | 90°00′00″ | 600.00 |
| B→C | 345°57′45″ | 412.31 |
| C→D | 261°52′12″ | 282.84 |
| D→A | 198°26′06″ | 316.23 |

---

## Example 1 — Latitude & departure of each leg

**`Lat = L·cos(Az)`, `Dep = L·sin(Az)`.**

- **A→B** (Az 90°): Lat = 600·cos 90° = **0.00**; Dep = 600·sin 90° = **+600.00**
- **B→C** (Az 345.9625°): Lat = 412.31·cos 345.9625° = **+400.00**; Dep = 412.31·sin 345.9625° = **−100.00**
- **C→D** (Az 261.8700°): Lat = 282.84·cos 261.87° = **−40.00**; Dep = 282.84·sin 261.87° = **−280.00**
- **D→A** (Az 198.4350°): Lat = 316.23·cos 198.435° = **−300.00**; Dep = 316.23·sin 198.435° = **−100.00**

**Check:** ΣLat = 0 + 400 − 40 − 300 = **+60.00 ft**; ΣDep = 600 − 100 − 280 − 100 = **+120.00 ft** (these are the misclosures used in Example 4).

**Calculator (TI-36X Pro):** put the calc in DEGREE mode. For a leg, key `L  ×  cos(  Az  )  =` for the latitude and `L  ×  sin(  Az  )  =` for the departure. Convert a DMS azimuth first with the `°’”` (DMS) entry, e.g. `345°57′45″` entered directly, then `cos`. **Casio fx-991:** identical; enter the DMS angle with the `°’”` key. **HP-35S:** `345.5745  →HR` converts H.MMSS to decimal degrees, then `COS` / `SIN`.

---

## Example 2 — The inverse: distance & azimuth between two points (R▸P)

Point P1 = (N 5,000.00, E 5,000.00); Point P2 = (N 5,400.00, E 4,900.00). Find distance and azimuth P1→P2.

1. `ΔN = 5400 − 5000 = +400.00`;  `ΔE = 4900 − 5000 = −100.00`
2. **Distance** `D = √(400² + 100²) = √170000 = 412.31 ft`
3. **Azimuth** `Az = atan2(ΔE, ΔN) = atan2(−100, +400) = −14.036° → +345.96°` (i.e. **345°57′45″**). ΔN +, ΔE − ⇒ NW quadrant, so bearing **N 14°02′15″ W**.

**Calculator R▸P (TI-36X Pro):** `2nd [R▸P]` opens `R▸Pr(` and `R▸Pθ(`. Key `R▸Pr( ΔE , ΔN )` → **412.31** (distance); `R▸Pθ( ΔE , ΔN )` → **−14.04°**, add 360° → 345.96°, then `▸DMS`. (Enter ΔE first as *x*, ΔN as *y* per the surveying convention.) **Casio fx-991:** `Pol(ΔE, ΔN)` returns r→variable X and θ→variable Y in one step. **HP-35S:** enter ΔN, ΔE and press `→POL`.

---

## Example 3 — Coordinates of a point from azimuth + distance (P▸R)

From A = (N 5,000.00, E 5,000.00), run **Az 198°26′06″ for 316.23 ft** to point D. Find D's coordinates.

1. `ΔN (Lat) = 316.23·cos 198.435° = −300.00`;  `ΔE (Dep) = 316.23·sin 198.435° = −100.00`
2. `N_D = 5000 + (−300.00) = 4,700.00`;  `E_D = 5000 + (−100.00) = 4,900.00`

**Calculator P▸R (TI-36X Pro):** `2nd [P▸R]` gives `P▸Rx(` and `P▸Ry(`. Key `P▸Rx( L , Az )` → **departure −100.00** (the *x* result); `P▸Ry( L , Az )` → **latitude −300.00** (the *y* result). Add to the start coordinates. **Casio fx-991:** `Rec(L, Az)` returns x (=ΔE) and y (=ΔN). **HP-35S:** enter L, Az; `→REC`.

---

## Example 4 — Misclosure & relative precision

From Example 1, ΣLat = +60.00 ft, ΣDep = +120.00 ft, perimeter P = 600.00 + 412.31 + 282.84 + 316.23 = 1,611.38 ft.

1. **Linear misclosure** `e = √(60² + 120²) = √(3600 + 14400) = √18000 = 134.16 ft` (this exaggerated example shows the method; real misclosures are tenths of a foot).
2. **Relative precision** `RP = P / e = 1611.38 / 134.16 = 12.01` → **≈ 1:12**. (A real 0.13-ft misclosure on this perimeter would give 1611/0.13 ≈ **1:12,400**.)

**Calculator:** misclosure is just `hypot(ΣLat, ΣDep)` — on the TI use `R▸Pr(ΣDep, ΣLat)` to get e in one keystroke. Report relative precision by dividing and rounding to a clean 1:N.

---

## Example 5 — Area by coordinates (shoelace)

Four corners (closed-loop): A(N 5000, E 5000), B(N 5000, E 5600), C(N 5400, E 5500), D(N 4700, E 4900). Using X = Easting, Y = Northing, and the cross form `A = ½|Σ(Xᵢ·Y_{i+1} − X_{i+1}·Yᵢ)|`:

| i | Xᵢ (E) | Yᵢ (N) | X_{i+1} | Y_{i+1} | Xᵢ·Y_{i+1} | X_{i+1}·Yᵢ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 5000 | 5000 | 5600 | 5000 | 25,000,000 | 28,000,000 |
| B | 5600 | 5000 | 5500 | 5400 | 30,240,000 | 27,500,000 |
| C | 5500 | 5400 | 4900 | 4700 | 25,850,000 | 29,160,000 |
| D | 4900 | 4700 | 5000 | 5000 | 24,500,000 | 23,500,000 |

Σ(Xᵢ·Y_{i+1}) = 105,590,000; Σ(X_{i+1}·Yᵢ) = 108,160,000. Difference = −2,570,000.

`A = ½·|−2,570,000| = 1,285,000 ft²`  → **÷ 43,560 = 29.50 acres.**

**Calculator tip:** there is no one-button shoelace on the TI/Casio — set it up as a running sum in the home screen, or use the matrix/list features to enter the products. The HP-35S survey program book includes a stored **AREA** routine that accepts sequential N,E inputs and returns acreage directly.

The signs come out on their own when you work from the azimuth. Watch them as you go.

title: Exam Tips & Calculator Strategy
content:
## Strategy for the computations area

![Directing the rod person from an occupied station during a traverse. Clear communication and good station geometry make a clean, checkable traverse.](/lessons/fs/photos/starr-crew-directing.jpg "Photo: Starr Surveying (field photo)")

- **COGO is the most learnable, highest-density point source on the FS.** The same two operations (forward P▸R, inverse R▸P) plus shoelace area cover most items. Drill them until they are reflexive — you should not be *thinking* about which key, only about the geometry.
- **Pace:** ~2.9 min/question overall. A clean inverse or a single latitude/departure should take under a minute; flag a long multi-leg traverse-adjustment problem and bank quick ones first.
- **Sketch first.** A 30-second vicinity sketch with the rough azimuth of each leg catches sign and quadrant errors before they cost you.

## Approved-calculator tricks (TI-36X Pro / Casio fx-991 / HP-35S)

- **Always confirm DEGREE mode** before any trig. A traverse in radian mode is the classic silent blunder.
- **R▸P does the inverse in two keystrokes:** distance = `R▸Pr(ΔE, ΔN)`, azimuth = `R▸Pθ(ΔE, ΔN)`. On Casio, `Pol(ΔE, ΔN)` returns both r and θ at once (stored in X and Y).
- **P▸R does the forward computation:** departure = `P▸Rx(L, Az)`, latitude = `P▸Ry(L, Az)`. On Casio, `Rec(L, Az)`.
- **Surveying convention:** enter ΔE (departure) as *x* and ΔN (latitude) as *y*, because azimuth is measured from **north (the y-axis)**. Get this backwards and your azimuth is reflected.
- **Normalize azimuth:** if R▸Pθ / atan2 returns a negative angle, **add 360°**; if it exceeds 360°, subtract 360°.
- **DMS ↔ decimal:** TI uses `°’”` for entry and `▸DMS` for output; Casio the same; HP-35S uses `→HR` (to decimal) and `→HMS` (to D.MMSS). Convert *before* trig and back *after* an inverse.
- **Store and recall** running northing/easting totals (TI `STO`/`RCL`, HP register chaining) so you don't re-key coordinates leg to leg — this both saves time and prevents transcription blunders.
- **Misclosure in one shot:** `e = R▸Pr(ΣDep, ΣLat)`.

## Common traps

- **Latitude uses cosine, departure uses sine** — memorize "**L**atitude–co**s**, **D**eparture–**s**in." Swapping them is the #1 COGO error.
- **Bowditch vs. transit:** Bowditch weights by **course length**; transit weights by **latitude/departure magnitude**. The exam may name the rule — use the one asked.
- **Sign of the correction:** the correction is the **negative** of the closure distributed out (you are removing the misclosure).
- **Relative precision is reported as 1:N**, with the **larger** number being **better**. Don't invert it.
- **Area sign:** the shoelace sum is negative for clockwise vertex order — always take the **absolute value**, then divide by 43,560 for acres.
- **Units:** watch ft vs. m and US survey-foot vs. international foot when a problem mixes systems.

## How the handbook helps

The NCEES FS Reference Handbook v2.5 gives the **inverse** (distance + the quadrant-constant azimuth form), **area by coordinates**, **straight-line / coordinate-geometry** relations, and the **bearing/azimuth** conventions verbatim. Know *where* each lives (Mathematical & Surveying-Related Formulas → Area formulas, and the Coordinate Geometry section) so you can confirm a formula in seconds instead of deriving it under time pressure.

title: Module Overview
content:
## Closing the loop: from coordinates to acreage, dirt, and alignment

![A horizontal curve on a highway. Route-surveying geometry — radius R, tangent T, external E, and central angle I — is one of the most heavily tested computation topics.](/lessons/fs/photos/m5-highway-curve.jpg "Photo: formulanone from Huntsville, United States — CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons")

Module 4 turned bearings and distances into coordinates and closed traverses. This module puts those coordinates to work on the three remaining staples of the **Survey Computations** area (17–26 of the 110 FS questions): **areas**, **volumes**, and **curves**. Together they account for a large, very learnable share of the computational points on the exam.

**Area** is what most boundary and subdivision work ultimately reports. You will compute it two ways: from **coordinates** (the shoelace / coordinate method, equivalent to the legacy double-meridian-distance approach) when every corner is known, and from a series of **field offsets** along a baseline (the **trapezoidal** and **Simpson's 1/3** rules) when the boundary is an irregular line — a stream bank, a road edge, a tract front. You will also **partition** parcels and move fluently between **square feet, acres, and hectares**.

**Volume** is the heart of construction-survey earthwork. Cross-sectional **end areas** taken at regular stations are combined by the **average-end-area** formula (and refined by the **prismoidal** formula), then divided by **27** to report **cubic yards** for cut/fill and haul.

**Curves** — both **horizontal** (circular) and **vertical** (parabolic) — define route alignments. For horizontal curves you will compute the interlocking elements **T, L, R, D, M, E, LC**, lay out stationing (**PC = PI − T**, **PT = PC + L**), and set points by **deflection angle**. For vertical curves you will compute **elevations** anywhere on an equal-tangent parabola and locate its **high or low point**.

**Every formula matches the NCEES FS Reference Handbook v2.5** (Area formulas, Earthwork, Horizontal circular curves, Vertical curves), so the on-screen exam reference will look exactly like what you drill here.

title: Key Concepts
content:
## Area by coordinates (shoelace)

When every corner of a parcel has coordinates (Northing, Easting), the enclosed area for vertices numbered **in order** around the polygon is:

`A = ½·|Σ Xᵢ(Y_{i+1} − Y_{i−1})|`  (handbook form), equivalently the cross-product form `A = ½·|Σ (Xᵢ·Y_{i+1} − X_{i+1}·Yᵢ)|`.

Use **X = Easting, Y = Northing**, close the polygon (the last vertex connects back to the first), and take the **absolute value** — a clockwise vertex order makes the signed sum negative. Divide ft² by **43,560** for acres. This is the modern equivalent of the legacy **DMD (double meridian distance)** method, which sums each course's DMD × latitude and gives the same answer; the FS may name either.

## Area from field offsets — irregular boundaries

When one side of a parcel is an irregular line, you run a straight **baseline** and measure **perpendicular offsets** hᵢ to the boundary at a **constant interval w**. Two integration rules then give the area between the baseline and the boundary:

- **Trapezoidal rule** (any number of offsets): treats the boundary as straight between offsets.
  `A = w·[(h₁ + hₙ)/2 + h₂ + h₃ + … + hₙ₋₁]`
- **Simpson's 1/3 rule** (needs an **odd number of offsets / even number of intervals**): fits parabolas through successive triples, more accurate for curving boundaries.
  `A = (w/3)·[h₁ + hₙ + 4·(sum of odd-position offsets) + 2·(sum of even-position offsets)]`
  where, counting offsets 1…n, the **interior odd-position** offsets (2nd, 4th, …) get the **×4** weight and the **interior even-position** offsets (3rd, 5th, …) get the **×2** weight. (If n is even, apply Simpson to the first n−1 offsets and add the last strip as a trapezoid.)

## Partitioning and unit conversions

- 1 acre = 43,560 ft² = 10 square chains; 1 acre = 0.404687 hectare; 1 hectare = 10,000 m².
- **Partition** problems split a parcel along a line of given direction or through a given point so the pieces have target areas — you set the area equation equal to the target and solve for the unknown dimension.

## Earthwork volumes

Cross-sections are cut at regular stations; each has a **cut or fill end area** A (ft²). Between two adjacent sections a distance **L** apart:

- **Average end area:** `V = L·(A₁ + A₂)/2` — the workhorse; slightly **over**estimates when sections taper.
- **Prismoidal formula:** `V = L·(A₁ + 4·Aₘ + A₂)/6`, where **Aₘ is the area of the section midway between** (computed from the *mid dimensions*, **not** the average of A₁ and A₂). More accurate; the difference is the **prismoidal correction**.
- **Cubic yards:** divide ft³ by **27**. Apply **shrinkage** (compacted fill needs more bank volume) or **swell** (excavated rock bulks up) factors when the problem gives them.

## Horizontal (circular) curves

A simple circular curve connects two tangents that meet at the **PI** (point of intersection) with **deflection/central angle I (or Δ)**. Key points: **PC** (point of curvature, where the curve begins), **PT** (point of tangency, where it ends), radius **R**. The interlocking elements:

- **Degree of curve (arc def.):** `D = 5,729.58/R` — the central angle subtending a 100-ft arc.
- **Tangent:** `T = R·tan(I/2)` (PI to PC = PI to PT).
- **Length:** `L = R·I·(π/180) = (I/D)·100` (along the arc).
- **Long chord:** `LC = 2R·sin(I/2)`; **Middle ordinate:** `M = R·(1 − cos(I/2))`; **External:** `E = R·(sec(I/2) − 1)`.
- **Stationing:** `PC = PI − T`, then `PT = PC + L` (note PT is found by adding the *arc length*, never by adding T twice).
- **Deflection angle** to any point on the curve = half the central angle subtended from the PC: for an arc length ℓ, deflection δ = (ℓ/L)·(I/2); the total deflection from PC to PT is exactly I/2.

## Vertical (parabolic) curves

An **equal-tangent parabola** joins a back grade **g₁** to a forward grade **g₂** over horizontal length **L**, beginning at the **PVC** and ending at the **PVT**, with the grades meeting at the **PVI**. Grades are decimals (e.g. +2% = +0.02). Measuring **x horizontally from the PVC**:

- **Elevation on the curve:** `Y = Y_PVC + g₁·x + [(g₂−g₁)/(2L)]·x²`
- **Tangent (grade-line) elevation:** `Y_PVC + g₁·x`; the **tangent offset** is `y = [(g₂−g₁)/(2L)]·x²`.
- **Rate of grade change:** `r = (g₂−g₁)/L` (per station or per foot, matching x's units).
- **High/low point:** where the curve grade is zero, at `x_m = −g₁/r = −g₁·L/(g₂−g₁)` from the PVC. A **crest** (high point) occurs when g₁ > g₂; a **sag** (low point) when g₁ < g₂. The high/low point exists on the curve only when g₁ and g₂ have **opposite signs**.

title: Essential Formulas
content:
## Area

| Method | Formula | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Coordinates (shoelace) | `A = ½·|Σ (Xᵢ·Y_{i+1} − X_{i+1}·Yᵢ)|` | X = E, Y = N; close the polygon; take \|·\| |
| Handbook form | `A = ½·|Σ Xᵢ(Y_{i+1} − Y_{i−1})|` | identical result |
| DMD method | `2A = Σ (DMDᵢ · Latᵢ)` | DMDᵢ = DMDᵢ₋₁ + Depᵢ₋₁ + Depᵢ; first DMD = first Dep |
| Trapezoidal rule | `A = w·[(h₁ + hₙ)/2 + Σ(interior h)]` | w = offset interval |
| Simpson's 1/3 rule | `A = (w/3)·[h₁ + hₙ + 4·Σ(h_odd) + 2·Σ(h_even)]` | needs odd # of offsets |

**Conversions:** 1 acre = 43,560 ft²; acres = ft²/43,560; 1 hectare = 10,000 m² = 2.47105 acres.

## Earthwork volume

| Method | Formula |
|---|---|
| Average end area | `V = L·(A₁ + A₂)/2` |
| Prismoidal | `V = L·(A₁ + 4·Aₘ + A₂)/6` |
| Pyramid / cone | `V = L·A/3` (one end area zero) |
| Cubic yards | `V(yd³) = V(ft³)/27` |

(L = distance between sections, ft; A = end area, ft²; Aₘ = mid-section area from mid dimensions.)

## Horizontal circular curve

Given any two of {R, D, I} plus stationing, everything follows:

| Element | Formula |
|---|---|
| Degree of curve (arc) | `D = 5,729.58/R` ; `R = 5,729.58/D` |
| Tangent | `T = R·tan(I/2)` |
| Length | `L = R·I·(π/180) = (I/D)·100` |
| Long chord | `LC = 2R·sin(I/2)` |
| Middle ordinate | `M = R·(1 − cos(I/2))` |
| External | `E = R·(sec(I/2) − 1) = R·(1/cos(I/2) − 1)` |
| Stationing | `PC = PI − T` ; `PT = PC + L` |
| Deflection to a point | `δ = (ℓ/L)·(I/2)` (total PC→PT deflection = I/2) |

(I in degrees; convert to radians for the length formula: L = R·toRad(I).)

## Vertical (equal-tangent parabolic) curve

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Elevation on curve | `Y = Y_PVC + g₁·x + [(g₂−g₁)/(2L)]·x²` |
| Tangent (grade) elevation | `Y_PVC + g₁·x` |
| Tangent offset | `y = [(g₂−g₁)/(2L)]·x²` ; at PVI: `E = [(g₂−g₁)/(2L)]·(L/2)²` |
| Rate of grade change | `r = (g₂ − g₁)/L` |
| High/low point from PVC | `x_m = −g₁/r = −g₁·L/(g₂ − g₁)` |

(Grades as decimals: +2% → +0.02. x and L in the same horizontal unit — feet, or stations.)

## A labeled horizontal circular curve

The figure shows a simple circular curve: the back tangent and forward tangent meet at **PI** with deflection angle **I**; the curve runs from **PC** to **PT** with radius **R** and tangent length **T**.

---

## Example 1 — Full horizontal curve from R and I

Given **R = 1,145.92 ft**, deflection **I = 24°00′00″**, and **PI at station 42+50.00**. Find D, T, L, LC, M, E, and the stationing of PC and PT.

1. **Degree of curve:** `D = 5,729.58/R = 5,729.58/1,145.92 = 5.0000°` (a 5° curve).
2. **Tangent:** `T = R·tan(I/2) = 1,145.92·tan(12°) = 1,145.92·0.21256 = 243.57 ft`.
3. **Length:** `L = R·I·(π/180) = 1,145.92·(24·π/180) = 1,145.92·0.418879 = 480.00 ft` (check: (I/D)·100 = (24/5)·100 = 480.00 ✓).
4. **Long chord:** `LC = 2R·sin(I/2) = 2·1,145.92·sin12° = 2,291.84·0.20791 = 476.50 ft`.
5. **Middle ordinate:** `M = R·(1 − cos12°) = 1,145.92·(1 − 0.97815) = 25.04 ft`.
6. **External:** `E = R·(sec12° − 1) = 1,145.92·(1.02234 − 1) = 25.60 ft`.
7. **Stationing:** `PC = PI − T = (42+50.00) − 243.57 = station 40+06.43`. `PT = PC + L = (40+06.43) + 480.00 = station 44+86.43`.

**Calculator (TI-36X Pro):** DEGREE mode. `1145.92 × tan( 12 ) =` → 243.57. For L either `1145.92 × 24 × π ÷ 180 =` or simply `(24 ÷ 5) × 100`. For E: `1145.92 × ( 1 ÷ cos(12) − 1 ) =`. **Casio fx-991:** identical keystrokes; the `×10ˣ`/`Ans` keys help chain. **HP-35S (RPN):** `12 TAN 1145.92 × ` gives T; enter I as 24, `→RAD`, `× R` for L.

---

## Example 2 — Deflection angle for staking the curve

Using the curve above (L = 480.00 ft, I = 24°), find the **deflection angle from the PC** to the curve point at the half-station **42+00**, and the chord from PC to it.

1. Arc from PC to 42+00: `ℓ = (42+00) − (40+06.43) = 193.57 ft`.
2. **Deflection:** `δ = (ℓ/L)·(I/2) = (193.57/480.00)·12° = 0.40327·12° = 4.839° = 4°50′21″`.
3. **Chord (from PC):** `c = 2R·sin(δ) = 2·1,145.92·sin(4.839°) = 2,291.84·0.08436 = 193.34 ft` (slightly less than the arc, as expected).

**Check:** the deflection from PC all the way to PT must be **I/2 = 12°00′00″** — a built-in field check. **Calculator:** compute δ in decimal degrees, then `▸DMS` for the field book.

---

## Example 3 — Vertical curve elevation and low point

A sag vertical curve has back grade **g₁ = −3.00%**, forward grade **g₂ = +2.00%**, length **L = 600.00 ft**, with **PVC at station 25+00, elevation 842.00 ft**. Find the elevation at station 28+00 and the station/elevation of the low point.

1. Grades as decimals: g₁ = −0.03, g₂ = +0.02. `x` at 28+00 = (28+00) − (25+00) = **300.00 ft**.
2. **Elevation on curve:** `Y = 842.00 + (−0.03)(300) + [(0.02 − (−0.03))/(2·600)]·300²`
   = 842.00 − 9.00 + [0.05/1200]·90,000 = 842.00 − 9.00 + 3.75 = **836.75 ft**.
3. **Low point from PVC:** `x_m = −g₁·L/(g₂ − g₁) = −(−0.03)(600)/(0.05) = 18/0.05 = 360.00 ft` → station **28+60**.
4. **Low-point elevation:** `Y = 842.00 + (−0.03)(360) + [0.05/1200]·360² = 842.00 − 10.80 + 5.40 = 836.60 ft`.

**Calculator:** store `a = (g₂−g₁)/(2L) = 0.05/1200 = 4.1667e−5` in memory, then `Y = 842 + (−0.03)x + a·x²` for any x. **Casio fx-991:** use the table (TABLE) mode with f(x) = 842 − 0.03x + 4.1667e−5·x² to print elevations at each station automatically.

---

## Example 4 — Area by coordinates (quad → acres)

A four-corner lot, vertices in order: A(N 1,000.00, E 1,000.00), B(N 1,000.00, E 1,400.00), C(N 1,300.00, E 1,400.00), D(N 1,300.00, E 1,000.00). Find the area in acres (X = E, Y = N).

| i | Xᵢ (E) | Yᵢ (N) | X_{i+1} | Y_{i+1} | Xᵢ·Y_{i+1} | X_{i+1}·Yᵢ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1000 | 1000 | 1400 | 1000 | 1,400,000 | 1,400,000 |
| B | 1400 | 1000 | 1400 | 1300 | 1,820,000 | 1,400,000 |
| C | 1400 | 1300 | 1000 | 1300 | 1,820,000 | 1,300,000 |
| D | 1000 | 1300 | 1000 | 1000 | 1,000,000 | 1,300,000 |

Σ(Xᵢ·Y_{i+1}) = 6,040,000; Σ(X_{i+1}·Yᵢ) = 5,400,000. Difference = 640,000.
`A = ½·|640,000| = 120,000 ft²` → **÷ 43,560 = 2.755 acres** (a 400 × 300 rectangle, as a sanity check).

---

## Example 5 — Average end area earthwork volume

Two adjacent cross-sections, 100.00 ft apart (one full station), have cut end areas **A₁ = 120.0 ft²** and **A₂ = 180.0 ft²**. Find the cut volume in cubic yards.

1. **Average end area:** `V = L·(A₁ + A₂)/2 = 100·(120 + 180)/2 = 100·150 = 15,000 ft³`.
2. **Cubic yards:** `V = 15,000 / 27 = 555.6 yd³`.

If the mid-section area were measured (say Aₘ = 148.0 ft²), the **prismoidal** volume would be `V = 100·(120 + 4·148 + 180)/6 = 100·892/6 = 14,866.7 ft³ = 550.6 yd³` — the **prismoidal correction** of about 5 yd³ less. **Calculator:** `100 × (120 + 180) ÷ 2 ÷ 27 =` → 555.6. Always divide ft³ by 27 last to report yards.

Every curve problem starts here. Run it until the constant is in your fingers.
