title: Exam Tips & Calculator Strategy
content:
## Strategy for areas, volumes, and curves

- **These are high-yield, formula-lookup points.** Every formula you need is in the handbook (Area formulas, Earthwork, Horizontal circular curves, Vertical curves). Know *where* each lives so you confirm rather than derive. Curves alone reliably appear several times.
- **Pace:** a single curve element (T, L, M, E) or one average-end-area volume is a sub-minute calculation; a full curve layout with stationing is a flag-and-return item. Bank the one-formula questions first.
- **Sketch the curve.** A quick PI–PC–PT sketch with I marked prevents the classic error of adding T (a straight distance) instead of L (the arc) when stationing the PT.

## Approved-calculator tricks (TI-36X Pro / Casio fx-991 / HP-35S)

- **Confirm DEGREE mode** before any curve trig. Then I/2 is just `I ÷ 2`; feed it straight into tan/cos/sin.
- **External and middle ordinate** both use I/2: `E = R(1/cos(I/2) − 1)`, `M = R(1 − cos(I/2))`. There is no `sec` key — type `1/cos(...)`.
- **Curve length two ways:** `L = R·toRad(I)` (radians) OR the cleaner `(I/D)·100`. Use the second when D is given — it avoids π entirely.
- **Vertical curves:** put grades in as **decimals** (+2% → 0.02). Store the constant `a = (g₂−g₁)/(2L)` once; then any elevation is `Y_PVC + g₁x + a·x²`. The Casio **TABLE** mode and TI **table** print a full elevation column in one setup.
- **Stationing arithmetic:** a station is just feet (42+50 = 4,250 ft). Do the math in feet, then re-split into stations (÷100 for the station number, remainder for the plus).
- **Volume:** keep everything in ft² and ft, then **÷27 at the very end** for cubic yards. Mixing the /27 in early is a common slip.
- **Area by offsets:** Simpson needs an **odd number of offsets**; if you're given an even number, Simpson the first n−1 and add the last strip as a trapezoid, or just use the trapezoidal rule.

## Common traps

- **PT = PC + L, not PC + 2T or PI + T.** The curve length is the arc; T is a straight tangent distance. This is the single most common curve blunder.
- **Degree of curve uses 5,729.58, not 5,730.** Arc definition. R = 5,729.58/D.
- **Prismoidal Aₘ** is computed from the **mid-section's own dimensions**, *not* the average (A₁+A₂)/2 — using the average just reproduces the end-area answer.
- **High/low point only exists when g₁ and g₂ have opposite signs.** A grade that goes −1% to −3% (both negative) has no turning point on the curve.
- **Average end area slightly over-estimates** volume for tapering sections; the prismoidal value is smaller (the correction). Know which the question wants.
- **Acres vs. square feet:** divide by **43,560**. Hectares: 1 ha = 10,000 m² = 2.47105 acres — watch SI vs. USCS.
- **Simpson weighting:** ends ×1, interior **odd-position** offsets ×4, interior **even-position** ×2 — miscounting the weights is the usual error.

## How the handbook helps

The NCEES FS Reference Handbook v2.5 gives the **horizontal circular curve** set (D, T, L, LC, M, E, stationing), the **vertical curve** parabola (elevation, tangent offset, rate r, high/low x_m), the **area formulas** (coordinates, trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3), and **earthwork** (average end area, prismoidal) verbatim. Practice pulling each up by name so that on exam day the formula is a confirmation, not a recall test.

title: Module Overview
content:
## Where geodesy and GNSS sit on the FS

The NCEES FS exam tests geodesy and GNSS under **Surveying Principles** (Area 4: basic surveying, geodesy, and *applied* geodesy — datums, datum conversions, SPCS, map projections, satellite coordinate systems) and under **Surveying Processes and Methods** (Area 1: GNSS/GPS surveys — static, kinematic, OPUS, real-time networks). Together these are roughly an eighth of the exam, and they are conceptually rich rather than calculation-heavy: most points come from *understanding* how a satellite position becomes a grid coordinate on a map.

This module follows the **measurement → reference frame → projection** chain that every modern survey rides:

1. **GNSS measures** a three-dimensional position relative to an **ellipsoid** (a smooth mathematical earth) in a global datum (WGS84 / NAD83 / the 2022 frames).
2. The height it returns is an **ellipsoidal height h**, not the **orthometric height H** (elevation above the **geoid**, the equipotential 'mean sea level' surface). The two are tied by the **geoid undulation N**: `H = h − N`.
3. To put the position on a flat **map** we apply a **projection** — Lambert Conformal Conic for east–west states, Transverse Mercator for north–south states — producing **State Plane** (or UTM) **grid coordinates**.
4. Grid coordinates are not ground distances. The **combined factor** (scale factor × elevation factor) converts between **grid** and **ground**, and **convergence** relates grid north to geodetic north.

Master the vocabulary (geoid vs. ellipsoid, datum vs. projection, grid vs. ground), the one essential height equation **H = h − N**, and the one essential distance chain **grid = ground × CSF**, and you will pick up most of the available points. Every formula here matches the **NCEES FS Reference Handbook v2.5** (Geodesy, State Plane Coordinates, and Conversions sections) so the on-screen reference will look familiar.

![A survey-grade GNSS receiver on a tripod. It tracks multiple satellite constellations to fix a precise position; results are ellipsoidal coordinates and heights that a geoid model converts to orthometric elevations.](/lessons/fs/photos/gnss-receiver.jpg "Photo: LubGua987, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons")

title: Key Concepts
content:
## GNSS fundamentals

**GNSS** (Global Navigation Satellite System) is the umbrella term; **GPS** is the U.S. constellation. The four major constellations are **GPS (USA)**, **GLONASS (Russia)**, **Galileo (EU)**, and **BeiDou (China)**. A receiver computes position by measuring **ranges** to satellites whose orbital positions are known from the broadcast **ephemeris**. Each constellation has three segments: **space** (satellites), **control** (ground monitoring/upload stations), and **user** (receivers).

![A GPS satellite in orbit. GNSS positioning trilaterates a ground position from simultaneous ranges to multiple satellites in view.](/lessons/fs/photos/m6-gps-constellation.jpg "Photo: NASA — Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons")

Two observable types:

- **Code (pseudorange)** — fast to acquire, meter-level; the basis of autonomous and DGPS navigation.
- **Carrier phase** — uses the wavelength of the carrier (~19 cm L1); millimeter-to-centimeter precision once the integer **ambiguity** is resolved. All high-accuracy surveying is carrier-phase.

A single receiver positioning by itself is **autonomous** (a few meters). Accuracy improves through **differencing** against a reference of known coordinates, which cancels common errors.

## Positioning (field) methods

| Method | Observable | Typical accuracy | When used |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Autonomous** | code | 2–5 m | navigation, recon |
| **DGPS / SBAS (WAAS)** | code (differential) | sub-meter to ~1 m | GIS, mapping-grade |
| **Static** | carrier, long occupation (20 min–hours) | mm–cm | control, long baselines |
| **Fast/rapid static** | carrier, short occupation | cm | densifying control |
| **RTK (real-time kinematic)** | carrier, base→rover radio | 1–3 cm | layout, topo, boundary |
| **PPK (post-processed kinematic)** | carrier, processed later | 1–3 cm | when no real-time link |
| **RTN / VRS (network RTK)** | carrier, modeled from a CORS network | 1–3 cm | RTK without your own base |
| **OPUS / PPP** | carrier, processed against CORS / precise orbits | cm | single-receiver static positioning |

**OPUS** (Online Positioning User Service, NGS) post-processes a single static occupation against the **CORS** (Continuously Operating Reference Stations) network and returns published NAD83 and ITRF coordinates. **PPP** (precise point positioning) uses precise satellite orbit/clock products to position a single receiver without a local base.

## GNSS error sources

- **Ionospheric delay** — frequency-dependent; largely removed by **dual-frequency** (L1/L2) receivers; the largest natural error.
- **Tropospheric delay** — modeled (not frequency-dependent); worse at low elevation angles.
- **Satellite clock & ephemeris (orbit) errors** — corrected by broadcast/precise products; differenced out over short baselines.
- **Multipath** — signal reflecting off nearby surfaces; mitigated by choke-ring antennas, siting, and avoiding reflective surfaces. **Not** reduced by differencing (it is site-specific).
- **Receiver noise** and **antenna phase-center variation**.
- **Cycle slips** — loss of carrier lock that must be repaired in processing.

## Dilution of Precision (DOP)

**DOP** quantifies how satellite *geometry* amplifies ranging error into position error. **Lower DOP is better** (well-spread satellites). Position error ≈ **UERE × DOP**, where **UERE** is the user-equivalent range error.

- **GDOP** (geometric, 3D + time), **PDOP** (position, 3D), **HDOP** (horizontal), **VDOP** (vertical), **TDOP** (time).
- VDOP is typically worse than HDOP because all satellites are above the horizon (no satellites 'below' to balance the vertical).

## Heights: geoid, ellipsoid, orthometric — H = h − N

Three surfaces:

- **Ellipsoid** — the smooth mathematical reference (GRS80 for NAD83). GNSS heights are **ellipsoidal heights h** measured along the ellipsoid normal.
- **Geoid** — the equipotential gravity surface approximating mean sea level; the reference for **orthometric height H** (the 'elevation' a level gives).
- **Geoid undulation N** — the separation between geoid and ellipsoid (negative across most of the conterminous U.S.).

**The single most-tested geodesy relationship:**

`H = h − N`   (equivalently `h = H + N`)

A **geoid model** (e.g., GEOID18, and the upcoming **GEOID2022**) supplies N so GNSS ellipsoidal heights can be converted to usable orthometric elevations.

## Datums and reference frames

- **NAD83** — the horizontal datum for U.S. surveying (uses the **GRS80** ellipsoid). Realized through CORS/HARN.
- **WGS84** — the GPS broadcast datum; now essentially coincident with ITRF at the ~cm level (NAD83 differs from WGS84/ITRF by 1–2 m due to plate motion and origin definition).
- **NAVD88** — the current vertical datum (orthometric).
- **GRS80** — the reference ellipsoid (a = 6,378,137 m, 1/f = 298.257222101).
- **2022 modernization (NGS)** — replaces NAD83 and NAVD88 with the **terrestrial reference frames** of the **North American Terrestrial Reference Frame of 2022 (NATRF2022)** (plus Pacific/Caribbean/Mariana frames) for horizontal and the **North American–Pacific Geopotential Datum of 2022 (NAPGD2022)** for vertical, with **GEOID2022** providing N. These are plate-fixed, time-dependent (epoch) frames aligned to the ITRF and realized largely by GNSS/CORS rather than passive marks.

## Map projections and SPCS

A **projection** flattens the curved ellipsoid onto a plane, introducing **distortion**; surveying uses **conformal** projections (angles preserved locally). Two families dominate U.S. State Plane:

- **Lambert Conformal Conic (LCC)** — a cone; best for zones that are **long east–west** (e.g., Texas zones, Pennsylvania).
- **Transverse Mercator (TM)** — a cylinder; best for zones **long north–south** (e.g., Illinois, New Jersey).
- (**Oblique Mercator** is used for the Alaska panhandle Zone 1.)

The **State Plane Coordinate System (SPCS)** divides each state into zones sized so the **scale distortion stays within about 1:10,000**. **UTM** (Universal Transverse Mercator) is a global TM system in 6°-wide zones; its central-meridian scale factor is fixed at **0.9996** (larger distortion than SPCS, so SPCS is preferred for local surveying).

## Grid vs. ground, and convergence

**Grid** distances/coordinates live on the projection; **ground** distances are what you measure with an EDM. Convert with the **combined factor**:

- **Scale factor (SF)** — projection distortion (ellipsoid → grid); near 1 (e.g., 0.9999).
- **Elevation (sea-level) factor (EF)** — reduces a ground distance to the ellipsoid: `EF = R/(R + H + N) ≈ R/(R + h)`, R ≈ 20,906,000 ft.
- **Combined scale factor:** `CSF = SF × EF`.
- **`grid = ground × CSF`**, and **`ground = grid / CSF`**.

**Convergence γ** (the **mapping angle**) is the angle between **grid north** and **geodetic (true) north** at a point; it grows with distance from the zone's central meridian. Grid azimuth = geodetic azimuth − γ + the small **arc-to-chord (t−T)** correction.

![GNSS gives ellipsoidal height h (above the reference ellipsoid). Orthometric height H (the elevation used for design and drainage) is measured above the geoid, and the geoid separation N relates them: h = H + N, so H = h − N.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/gnss-heights.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![GNSS positioning by trilateration: measured ranges to at least four satellites fix the receiver's position (X, Y, Z), with the fourth range solving the receiver clock bias.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/gnss-trilateration.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![Ground vs. grid distance: the ground distance is scaled to the ellipsoid by the elevation factor, then to the state-plane grid by the scale factor; their product is the combined (grid) factor, so grid distance = ground distance × combined factor.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/grid-ground.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![Height systems: the ellipsoidal height h (from GNSS) equals the orthometric height H (above the geoid) plus the geoid height N (geoid–ellipsoid separation): h = H + N.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/geoid-height-systems.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep (generated)")

title: Essential Formulas
content:
## Heights (NCEES Handbook — Geodesy)

| Quantity | Formula | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Height relationship | `h = H + N`  →  `H = h − N` | h = ellipsoidal, H = orthometric, N = geoid undulation |
| Geoid undulation | `N = h − H` | from a geoid model (GEOID18 / GEOID2022) |

**Memory hook:** ellipsoidal (GNSS) is 'higher up the alphabet' — `h = H + N`. To get the elevation you *subtract* the (usually negative) undulation: `H = h − N`.

## Distance reduction chain (SPCS — Handbook State Plane section)

| Step | Formula |
|---|---|
| Elevation (sea-level) factor | `EF = R / (R + H + N) ≈ R / (R + h)`,  R ≈ 20,906,000 ft |
| Projection scale factor | `SF` (from the zone's projection / published value) |
| Combined scale factor | `CSF = SF × EF` |
| Ground → grid | `D_grid = D_ground × CSF` |
| Grid → ground | `D_ground = D_grid / CSF` |
| Ellipsoid (geodetic) distance | `D_E = D_ground × EF` (ground → ellipsoid) |
| Arc-to-chord (t−T) | `AR − CH = CH³ / (24R²)` |

(For precision looser than ~1:200,000 you may use R ≈ 20,906,000 ft and neglect N, so `EF ≈ R/(R+H)`.)

## GNSS error budget and DOP

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Baseline error budget | `σ = a + b·L`  (a in mm, b in ppm, L in km) |
| Position error from DOP | `σ_pos = UERE × DOP`  (use HDOP, VDOP, or PDOP for the matching component) |
| Geometric range, satellite→receiver | `ρ = √((Xs−Xr)² + (Ys−Yr)² + (Zs−Zr)²)` |

## Ellipsoid geometry (Handbook — Geodesy)

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Flattening | `f = (a − b)/a`  (published as 1/f) |
| Eccentricity² | `e² = (a² − b²)/a²` |
| Radius in the meridian | `M = a(1 − e²)/(1 − e²·sin²φ)^{3/2}` |
| Radius in the prime vertical | `N_pv = a/(1 − e²·sin²φ)^{1/2}` |
| GRS80 ellipsoid | a = 6,378,137.0 m, 1/f = 298.257222101 |
| Orthometric correction | `−0.005288·sin 2φ·Δφ·(arc 1′)` |

## Convergence / azimuth

`Az_grid = Az_geodetic − γ + (t − T)`

γ = convergence (mapping angle, grid north relative to geodetic north); (t − T) = arc-to-chord correction (small, often negligible for short lines).

title: Worked Examples
content:
## The measurement-to-map chain, illustrated

![A permanent GNSS reference-station antenna (a CORS). Continuously operating reference stations provide the base observations for RTK and post-processed positioning.](/lessons/fs/photos/m6-cors-antenna.jpg "Photo: Karlbrix — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons")

<svg width="480" height="260" viewBox="0 0 480 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#fff;border:1px solid #ccc">
  <!-- terrain -->
  <path d="M20,70 Q140,40 260,75 T460,70" fill="none" stroke="#7a5230" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="24" y="62" font-size="12" fill="#7a5230">Ground (terrain), height H above geoid</text>
  <!-- geoid -->
  <path d="M20,150 Q140,140 260,152 T460,150" fill="none" stroke="#1c4e80" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="24" y="168" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">Geoid (≈ MSL) — datum for orthometric H</text>
  <!-- ellipsoid -->
  <line x1="20" y1="200" x2="460" y2="200" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
  <text x="24" y="218" font-size="12" fill="#555">Ellipsoid (GRS80) — datum for ellipsoidal h (GNSS)</text>
  <!-- vertical ties at x=300 -->
  <line x1="300" y1="73" x2="300" y2="200" stroke="#333" stroke-width="1"/>
  <line x1="300" y1="73" x2="300" y2="152" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="3"/>
  <text x="305" y="120" font-size="12" fill="#c0392b">H (orthometric)</text>
  <line x1="300" y1="152" x2="300" y2="200" stroke="#1c4e80" stroke-width="3"/>
  <text x="305" y="180" font-size="12" fill="#1c4e80">N (undulation)</text>
  <text x="360" y="140" font-size="12" fill="#333">h = H + N</text>
  <circle cx="300" cy="73" r="3" fill="#000"/>
  <text x="308" y="70" font-size="11">survey point</text>
</svg>

---

## Example 1 — Orthometric height from a GNSS observation (H = h − N)

A GNSS survey gives an **ellipsoidal height h = 1,250.00 ft** at a station. The geoid model returns a **geoid undulation N = −29.50 ft** there. Find the **orthometric height (elevation) H**.

`H = h − N = 1,250.00 − (−29.50) = 1,279.50 ft`

**Why it's larger:** N is negative across most of the lower-48, so the ellipsoid sits *above* the geoid; subtracting a negative undulation *adds* to the elevation. **Calculator (any approved model):** simply `1250 − (−29.5) =`. The only trap is the **sign of N** — read it off the geoid model exactly.

---

## Example 2 — Geoid undulation from known h and H

A benchmark has a published **orthometric elevation H = 612.40 ft** (NAVD88). A static GNSS occupation gives **h = 587.10 ft**. Find the **geoid undulation N** at the mark.

`N = h − H = 587.10 − 612.40 = −25.30 ft`

This is exactly how a GNSS-on-benchmarks campaign *measures* the geoid to validate a model. **Sanity check:** N is negative (typical for the conterminous U.S.), and |N| is a few tens of feet — reasonable.

---

## Example 3 — Combined factor and ground → grid distance

At a project site the **projection scale factor SF = 0.9999012** and the station elevation is **H = 4,500 ft** (geoid undulation small, neglected). Reduce a measured **ground distance of 2,456.78 ft** to a **grid distance** for State Plane.

1. **Elevation factor** `EF = R/(R + H) = 20,906,000 / (20,906,000 + 4,500) = 0.9997848`.
2. **Combined factor** `CSF = SF × EF = 0.9999012 × 0.9997848 = 0.9996860`.
3. **Grid distance** `D_grid = D_ground × CSF = 2,456.78 × 0.9996860 = 2,456.01 ft`.

**Calculator (TI-36X Pro / Casio fx-991):** compute EF, store it (`STO`), multiply by SF for CSF, then multiply the ground distance. The grid distance is **shorter** here because both factors are < 1 (elevation > sea level *and* this zone projects slightly small). **Trap:** at high elevations EF can dominate; near the standard parallels SF can exceed 1.

---

## Example 4 — Grid → ground (the reverse reduction)

State Plane inversed a line as **grid distance 2,456.78 ft**. The combined factor for the area is **CSF = 0.9998765**. What **ground distance** would you stake?

`D_ground = D_grid / CSF = 2,456.78 / 0.9998765 = 2,457.08 ft`

To go from grid back to ground you **divide** by the combined factor (the inverse of grid = ground × CSF). The ground distance is slightly **longer**, by about 0.30 ft over this line — exactly the kind of error that shows up when crews stake grid coordinates without applying the factor.

---

## Example 5 — Baseline error budget and DOP

**(a) Baseline accuracy.** A receiver pair is specified at **a = 5 mm + 1 ppm**. For a **12.34 km** baseline, the expected horizontal uncertainty is:

`σ = a + b·L = 5 mm + (1 ppm)(12.34 km) = 5 + 1×12.34 = 17.34 mm` (≈ 0.017 m).

(1 ppm = 1 mm per km, so b·L = 12.34 mm.)

**(b) Position error from DOP.** If the **UERE ≈ 2.5 m** and the current **PDOP = 3.2**, the expected 3-D position error is:

`σ_pos = UERE × PDOP = 2.5 × 3.2 = 8.0 m`.

**Takeaway:** wait for a **low DOP** window — the same ranging error produces far smaller position error when the satellite geometry is strong. **Calculator:** both are one-line multiplications; the only skill is matching the right DOP (HDOP/VDOP/PDOP) to the component asked.

---

## Example 6 — Convergence and grid azimuth (concept-to-number)

At a station the **convergence (mapping angle) γ = +1°12′30″** and the (t−T) arc-to-chord correction is negligible. A line has a **geodetic azimuth of 87°45′00″**. The **grid azimuth** is:

`Az_grid = Az_geodetic − γ = 87°45′00″ − 1°12′30″ = 86°32′30″`.

Convergence is **positive east of the central meridian** (grid north lies west of true north there), so grid azimuths come out *smaller* than geodetic. **Calculator:** subtract in DMS mode (TI/Casio `°’”`).

title: Exam Tips & Calculator Strategy
content:
## Strategy for the geodesy / GNSS area

![A Starr Surveying GNSS rover with data collector. RTK positioning fixes coordinates in seconds — but you still need to understand datums, geoid height, and check shots.](/lessons/fs/photos/starr-gnss-rover.jpg "Photo: Starr Surveying (field photo)")

- **This is a vocabulary-and-concept area first, a math area second.** Most points come from knowing *which surface, datum, projection, or method* is correct — fast questions you should bank early in the exam. The few calculations (H = h − N, grid = ground × CSF) are one-liners.
- **Lock down the three surfaces.** Ellipsoid (GNSS h), geoid (orthometric H, ≈ MSL), and the undulation N between them. If you can recite `H = h − N` and explain why N is usually negative in the U.S., you own the most-tested item.
- **Datum vs. projection vs. coordinate system** are different things: a *datum* (NAD83) defines the reference frame; a *projection* (Lambert / Transverse Mercator) flattens it; SPCS/UTM are *coordinate systems* built on a projection. Watch questions that swap these.
- **Know the projection-to-state shape rule:** **Lambert Conformal Conic for east–west zones, Transverse Mercator for north–south zones.** Texas (wide E–W) uses Lambert.
- **Currency:** the FS still references NAD83/NAVD88, but be ready for one item on the **2022 modernization** — NATRF2022 (horizontal), NAPGD2022 (vertical), GEOID2022 — which replaces passive monuments with GNSS/CORS-realized, time-dependent frames.

## Approved-calculator tricks (TI-36X Pro / Casio fx-991 / HP-35S)

- **EF and CSF are short chains — store intermediates.** Compute `EF = R/(R+H)`, `STO` it, multiply by SF for CSF, then by the distance. Re-keying R = 20,906,000 ft each time invites blunders; store it once.
- **Direction of the factor:** **ground → grid = multiply; grid → ground = divide.** Sanity-check: at elevation, ground is longer than grid, so the ground number should be the bigger one.
- **DMS for convergence:** enter γ and azimuths with the `°’”` (TI/Casio) key; HP-35S uses `→HR`/`→HMS`. Keep the calculator in **DEGREE** mode.
- **ppm is mm-per-km:** `b ppm × L km` gives millimeters directly — no unit gymnastics. Add the constant term `a` (also mm).
- **DOP is a pure multiplier:** `σ_pos = UERE × DOP`. Match HDOP to horizontal, VDOP to vertical, PDOP to 3-D.

## Common traps

- **Sign of N:** `H = h − N`. With N negative (typical U.S.), the orthometric height ends up *larger* than the ellipsoidal height. Flip the sign and you lose the point.
- **Multiply vs. divide the combined factor:** grid = ground × CSF; ground = grid ÷ CSF.
- **Lower DOP is better.** A 'high DOP' (poor geometry) inflates position error — don't pick it as the 'good' condition.
- **Multipath is not removed by differencing** (it is site-specific); the dual-frequency cure is for the *ionosphere*.
- **UTM scale factor is fixed 0.9996** at the central meridian; SPCS zones are tighter (~1:10,000), which is *why* SPCS is preferred for local work.
- **Ellipsoidal height ≠ elevation.** A GNSS 'height' is not an orthometric elevation until you apply the geoid model.
- **WGS84 vs. NAD83** differ by 1–2 m — they are not interchangeable for survey-grade work even though both use ~GRS80-class ellipsoids.

## How the handbook helps

The NCEES FS Reference Handbook v2.5 gives, verbatim: the **height relationship h = H + N** and ellipsoid constants (Geodesy section); the **State Plane** distance-reduction chain (`EF = R/(R+H+N)`, combined factor, arc-to-chord); GRS80/Clarke-1866 ellipsoid parameters; and the unit conversions (R ≈ 20,906,000 ft ≈ 6,372,000 m). Know *where* each lives so you can confirm a factor in seconds instead of deriving it under time pressure.

title: Module Overview
content:
## The heaviest area on the FS exam

![A set boundary monument. Physical monuments are the highest form of evidence for a property corner — they generally control over record distances and bearings.](/lessons/fs/photos/m7-boundary-monument.jpg "Photo: Osumi Akari — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons")

**Boundary Law and Real Property Principles is the single largest knowledge area on the NCEES FS exam — 19 to 29 of the 110 questions (roughly 17–26%).** Do not treat the FS as a pure math test: more points live here than in any computational area, and most boundary questions are conceptual, fast to answer, and high-return. A candidate who masters this module banks a large block of quick points while others burn time on long COGO problems.

Boundary law answers one question: **where is the line, and who owns the land?** It is answered with three intertwined systems:

1. **The Public Land Survey System (PLSS)** — the federal rectangular grid of townships, ranges, sections, and **aliquot parts** that organizes most of the 30 "public-land states." You must be able to number a section, subdivide it, compute aliquot-part acreage, and **restore a lost corner** by single or double proportionate measurement using the BLM *Manual of Surveying Instructions*.

2. **Legal descriptions** — **metes-and-bounds** (a perimeter of bearings, distances, and monuments), **lot-and-block** (reference to a recorded subdivision plat), and **PLSS aliquot** (e.g., the *NE¼ of the SW¼ of Sec. 14*). Each must unambiguously locate one closed parcel.

3. **Common-law boundary doctrine** — the **dignity (priority) of calls**, the **footsteps of the original surveyor**, **senior/junior rights**, **simultaneous vs. sequential** conveyances, **water boundaries** (riparian/littoral, accretion/avulsion), **adverse possession**, **easements**, and **recording/chain of title**.

Throughout, watch for **Texas specifics**: Texas was **never federal public domain**, so **most of Texas has no PLSS township-range grid** — Texas land is metes-and-bounds keyed to an **original General Land Office (GLO) survey + abstract number**, measured historically in **varas**. These Texas-vs-PLSS distinctions are flagged in callouts and appear on the Texas SIT. Every concept here is exam-aligned to the NCEES FS specification (Area 3) and the supplied standards.

title: Key Concepts
content:
## 1. The Public Land Survey System (PLSS)

The PLSS (begun under the Land Ordinance of 1785, administered today by the **BLM**, successor to the federal **General Land Office**) lays a **rectangular grid** over the public domain. It is built from an **initial point**, from which run a **principal meridian** (north–south) and a **base line** (east–west).

- **Township strips** run east–west, numbered north or south of the base line: **T2N, T3S**, etc.
- **Range strips** run north–south, numbered east or west of the principal meridian: **R4E, R1W**, etc.
- A **township** is the 6 mi × 6 mi square at the intersection of a township row and a range column — nominally **36 sq miles**, containing **36 sections**.

**Section numbering is a boustrophedon ("ox-plow") serpentine:** Section 1 is in the **NE corner**, numbering runs **west** across the top to 6, **drops down** to 7, runs **east** to 12, drops to 13, and so on, ending at **Section 36 in the SE corner**.

```
  6  5  4  3  2  1
  7  8  9 10 11 12
 18 17 16 15 14 13
 19 20 21 22 23 24
 30 29 28 27 26 25
 31 32 33 34 35 36
```

A **standard section is 1 mile square = 640 acres.** Because the Earth converges toward the poles, the grid cannot be perfectly square: **standard parallels (correction lines)** and **guide meridians** periodically reset the grid, and the resulting deficiency or surplus is thrown into the **west and north tiers** of the township as irregular **government lots** (e.g., along a meander line or the township's NW corner). Sections 6 and along the north/west edges therefore commonly contain fractional government lots rather than clean aliquot parts.

## 2. Aliquot parts and section subdivision

A section is subdivided by repeated halving and quartering into **aliquot parts**. The acreage of any aliquot part is simply the **product of its fractions times 640 acres**:

- **Quarter section** (NE¼) = ¼ × 640 = **160 acres**
- **Quarter-quarter** (NE¼ of the NW¼), the classic **"forty"** = ¼ × ¼ × 640 = **40 acres**
- **Half of a quarter** (N½ of the NW¼) = ½ × ¼ × 640 = **80 acres**
- **Half-half-quarter** (S½ of the NE¼ of the SW¼) = ½ × ¼ × ¼ × 640 = **20 acres**

**Read the description right-to-left** to nest the parts: "the *NE¼ of the SW¼*" means *take the SW quarter (160 ac), then its NE quarter (40 ac)*. The center-quarter corners and quarter-quarter corners are set by **straight lines connecting opposite quarter and sixteenth corners** on the section boundary (the BLM "3-3 rule" of subdivision), **not** by measuring nominal 1,320-ft distances — found original corners control, and any excess/deficiency falls into the northern/western lots.

## 3. Existent, obliterated, and lost corners

When retracing a PLSS line you must classify each original corner:

- **Existent corner** — its position can be recovered from the original monument or undisturbed accessories, beyond reasonable doubt. **It controls; never disturb it.**
- **Obliterated corner** — no trace of the monument remains, **but its position can be recovered from collateral evidence** (testimony, fences/occupation lines, bearing trees, found accessories, adjoiner deeds). An obliterated corner is **not** lost.
- **Lost corner** — its position **cannot be recovered from any acceptable evidence**, original or collateral, and can be restored **only by proportionate measurement** from surrounding existent corners. Proportioning is a **last resort.**

**Corner accessories** — **bearing trees** (scribed trees with recorded bearings/distances to the corner), **mounds, pits, and memorial objects** — are the surveyor's primary collateral evidence for recovering an obliterated corner.

## 4. Proportionate measurement

Proportionate measurement restores a **lost** corner so the restored point bears the **same ratio to the corrected whole as the record interval bears to the record whole**, distributing the accumulated discrepancy uniformly.

- **Single proportionate measurement ("two-way")** — for a corner that lies on **one line** between two found corners (e.g., a quarter corner between two section corners, or a lost corner on a township exterior). Distribute the measured-vs-record difference along that single line:  `d' = D_record × (L_measured / L_record)`.
- **Double proportionate measurement** — for a corner **controlled in two directions** (the typical **interior section corner**, common to four sections, controlled by the nearest found corners **north, south, east, and west**). Proportion **independently** in the N–S direction and the E–W direction to get two trial positions, then the corner is set at the intersection (the latitudinal value from the E–W proportion, the longitudinal value from the N–S proportion).

**Order of precedence is the exam point:** existent monuments → obliterated corners recovered by collateral evidence → **only then** lost-corner proportioning. A gross **blunder** is placed where it belongs; only ordinary distributed error is proportioned.

## 5. Legal descriptions

- **Metes-and-bounds** — a perimeter run: a **point of beginning (POB)**, a series of **calls** (bearing + distance), **monuments**, and closure back to the POB. The original system of the 13 colonies and of Texas.
- **Lot-and-block (platted)** — references a **recorded subdivision plat**: "Lot 7, Block 3, of Sunset Addition, recorded in Vol. __, Pg. __." The plat (a **simultaneous** conveyance) controls; lots have no seniority among themselves.
- **PLSS aliquot** — "the SE¼ of the NW¼ of Sec. 14, T2N, R3E, [meridian]." Compact and self-locating within the grid.

## 6. Dignity (priority) of calls and footsteps

When the calls in one description **conflict**, they are ranked by relative reliability ("dignity"), highest to lowest:

1. **Calls for natural monuments** (rivers, lakes, established trees, rock outcrops)
2. **Calls for artificial monuments** (set iron, stakes, marked trees, fences, road ROW)
3. **Calls for adjoinder** (an adjacent, already-established survey line)
4. **Course** (bearing/direction)
5. **Distance**
6. **Quantity / area / acreage** (the **weakest** — a check, not a control)

This hierarchy is **only a rule of construction** — a set of rebuttable presumptions — that **always yields to (i) the intent of the parties** (read within the four corners of the instrument) **and (ii) the footsteps of the original surveyor**: the line is located **where it was actually run on the ground**, even against later "more accurate" measurements. A found, identifiable original monument controls over conflicting course-and-distance calls.

## 7. Senior/junior rights; simultaneous vs. sequential

- **Sequential conveyances** (parcels carved off one at a time over time): **senior rights govern.** The **senior** (earlier) deed takes the full measure of its description; the **junior** (later) takes only the **remainder** — it absorbs any excess and eats any deficiency. **No proration.**
- **Simultaneous conveyances** (all parcels created at one instant — classically, lots in a recorded plat): **no lot is senior.** Excess or deficiency found between controlling monuments is **apportioned proportionately** among the affected lots by their record dimensions. The order lots later *sold* is immaterial.

## 8. Water boundaries

- **Riparian** rights attach to land along a **flowing watercourse**; **littoral** rights attach to land along a **static body** (lake, sea).
- On a **non-navigable** stream, the abutting owner generally takes to the **center thread**; on a **navigable** stream the bed below the ordinary high-water mark is **State-owned** (public-trust).
- **Accretion** (gradual deposit) and **reliction** (gradual uncovering) **move the boundary** — the owner gains. **Erosion** moves it landward — the owner loses. **Avulsion** (a **sudden**, perceptible change — a flood cutting a new channel) **FIXES the boundary** at its former location.

## 9. Adverse possession, easements, recording

- **Adverse possession** matures title in a trespasser whose possession is **actual, open and notorious, exclusive, hostile (under a claim of right), and continuous** for the statutory period. (Texas instead runs a **statutory multi-track** 3/5/10/25-year scheme in Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code Ch. 16.)
- **Easements** are **non-possessory** rights to use another's land — created **expressly** (writing), by **implication/prior use**, by **necessity**, or by **prescription** (adverse use for the statutory period). An **appurtenant** easement runs with the land; an **easement in gross** is personal.
- **Recording acts** give later purchasers notice and set priority. Three regimes: **race** (first to record wins), **notice** (a later bona-fide purchaser without notice wins, recording order irrelevant), and **race-notice** (later BFP wins only if without notice **and** records first). A **bona-fide purchaser (BFP)** pays value, in good faith, without actual or constructive notice.

![PLSS aliquot parts: a section is 640 acres (1 mile square). A quarter section is 160 acres and a quarter-quarter is 40 acres. Aliquot descriptions read right-to-left (e.g., the NW¼ of the NE¼ = 40 ac).](/lessons/fs/diagrams/plss-section.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![A metes-and-bounds description: bearing-and-distance calls run from the point of beginning (POB) around the tract and must close back on it — the Texas/colonial method, in contrast to the PLSS.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/metes-and-bounds.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![A recorded plat with lots along a street and monuments A and B at the block ends: the full lots hold their record frontage and the remainder lot absorbs the measured excess or deficiency.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/recorded-plat-lots.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep (generated)")

Turn the plat until its north arrow is up the page, then look at what happened to the bearing.

title: Essential Formulas & Reference Facts
content:
## PLSS dimensions and acreage

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Township | 6 mi × 6 mi = 36 sq mi = **36 sections** |
| Standard section | 1 mi × 1 mi = **640 acres** |
| Half section (N½, E½, …) | ½ × 640 = **320 acres** |
| Quarter section (NE¼, …) | ¼ × 640 = **160 acres** |
| Half-quarter (N½ of NW¼) | ½ × ¼ × 640 = **80 acres** |
| Quarter-quarter ("forty") | ¼ × ¼ × 640 = **40 acres** |
| Quarter-quarter-quarter (S½ of NE¼ of SW¼) | ½ × ¼ × ¼ × 640 = **20 acres** |

**General aliquot rule:**  `Area (acres) = (product of all the aliquot fractions) × 640`.

**Linear:** 1 section side = 1 mile = **80 chains = 5,280 ft**; a quarter-section side = ½ mile = 40 chains = **2,640 ft**; a quarter-quarter side = ¼ mile = 20 chains = **1,320 ft**.

## Units (NCEES handbook v2.5)

| Conversion | Value |
|---|---|
| 1 acre | **43,560 ft²** = 10 sq chains |
| 1 chain | 100 links = **66 ft** = 4 rods/poles/perches |
| 1 mile | 80 chains = **5,280 ft** |
| 1 acre | 0.40469 hectare |
| 1 sq mile | 640 acres |

## Single proportionate measurement

A lost corner on a single line between two found corners (1 and 2). Let `L_record` = total record distance 1→2, `L_measured` = total measured distance 1→2, `D_record` = record distance from corner 1 to the lost corner. The corrected (restored) distance from corner 1 is:

`d' = D_record × (L_measured / L_record)`

Equivalently, restore each coordinate of the lost corner by linear interpolation between the found corners' coordinates in proportion to the record distances:

`C_restored = C₁ + (C₂ − C₁) × (D_record / L_record)`

## Double proportionate measurement

For an interior corner controlled in two directions, proportion **separately**:
- **Latitude (N–S) value** from the nearest found corners **N and S**, by their record N–S distances.
- **Departure (E–W) value** from the nearest found corners **E and W**, by their record E–W distances.

The corner is set at the point having the proportioned **latitude** (from the N–S line) and the proportioned **departure** (from the E–W line). (A small final adjustment for the cardinal-offset is made per the BLM Manual; for FS purposes the two-direction proportion is the key idea.)

## Dignity of calls (memorize the order)

`Natural monuments  >  Artificial monuments  >  Adjoinder  >  Course  >  Distance  >  Quantity/area`

All subordinate to **(i) intent of the parties** and **(ii) footsteps of the original surveyor.**

## Water-boundary changes

| Process | Speed | Effect on boundary |
|---|---|---|
| **Accretion** | gradual addition | boundary **moves** (owner gains) |
| **Reliction** | gradual uncovering | boundary **moves** (owner gains) |
| **Erosion** | gradual loss | boundary **moves** (owner loses) |
| **Avulsion** | **sudden** change | boundary **FIXED** at former line |

## Texas conversions (callout)

| Unit | Value |
|---|---|
| **1 vara** | 33⅓ in = **2.7778 ft** (36 varas = exactly 100 ft) |
| Vara → feet | × 2.7778  (equivalently **÷ 0.36**) |
| Feet → vara | × **0.36** |
| 1 labor | 1,000,000 sq varas ≈ **177.1 acres** |
| 1 league (sitio) | 25,000,000 sq varas = 25 labors ≈ **4,428 acres** |
| League + labor | ≈ **4,605.5 acres** (standard married-head grant) |

> **⚠️ Texas vs. PLSS:** Most of Texas has **no township-range grid.** Texas grants are **metes-and-bounds keyed to an original GLO survey + abstract number**, measured in varas. Do not read a Texas description in T/R/Section terms, and do not apply a non-Texas vara value to a Texas grant.

---

## Example 1 — Acreage of an aliquot part

**Find the area of the *S½ of the NE¼ of the SW¼* of a regular section.**

Multiply the fractions, then × 640:

`A = ½ × ¼ × ¼ × 640 = (1/32) × 640 = 20.00 acres.`

**Method:** read right-to-left — the SW¼ (160 ac), its NE¼ (40 ac), the S½ of that (20 ac). A clean way to do it on the calculator: `640 ÷ 2 ÷ 4 ÷ 4 =` → **20**. (Each "half" divides by 2, each "quarter" divides by 4.)

**Calculator (TI-36X Pro / Casio fx-991):** `640 ÷ 2 ÷ 4 ÷ 4 =` returns **20**. No mode setting needed — this is pure arithmetic.

---

## Example 2 — A compound description

**Find the area of the *N½ of the NW¼* plus the *SE¼ of the NW¼*.**

- N½ of NW¼ = ½ × ¼ × 640 = **80 acres**
- SE¼ of NW¼ = ¼ × ¼ × 640 = **40 acres**
- **Total = 80 + 40 = 120 acres.**

Note the whole NW¼ is 160 ac; this description takes the north half (80) plus one of the two southern forties (40) = 120, leaving the SW¼NW¼ (40 ac) out.

---

## Example 3 — Dimensions of a forty

**A quarter-quarter (40-acre "forty") of a regular section is nominally how many feet on a side, and how many square feet?**

- Side = ¼ mile = 20 chains = 20 × 66 = **1,320 ft.**
- Area = 1,320 × 1,320 = 1,742,400 ft²; ÷ 43,560 = **40.00 acres** ✓ (the check).

**Calculator:** `1320 x² =` → 1,742,400, then `÷ 43560 =` → **40**. (Remember a forty is a square 1,320 ft on a side only in the *ideal* regular section; found original corners govern the real dimensions.)

---

## Example 4 — Single proportionate measurement (lost corner on one line)

A **quarter corner** is recorded **40.00 chains** from each adjacent **section corner** (record line length 80.00 ch). The quarter corner is **lost**. You remeasure the full line between the two **existent section corners** and get **80.40 chains** (40-link surplus). Where do you set the restored quarter corner?

1. **Proportion the record distance:** `d' = D_record × (L_measured / L_record) = 40.00 × (80.40 / 80.00) = 40.00 × 1.005 = 40.20 chains` from the first section corner.
2. So the restored quarter corner is **40.20 ch** from each section corner — the **0.40-ch surplus is split equally** (0.20 ch to each half), exactly because the record split was 40/40.

**Why proportion, not hold record?** The corner is *lost*, so no monument controls; single proportion distributes the accumulated surplus uniformly along the single line so neither half absorbs it all.

**Calculator:** `40 × ( 80.40 ÷ 80 ) =` → **40.20**. (In coordinates: restored N,E = section-corner-1 coordinates + 0.5 × (corner-2 − corner-1), since the record fraction is 40/80 = 0.5.)

---

## Example 5 — Coordinate form of single proportion (unequal record split)

Found corner **1** is at (N 1,000.00, E 1,000.00); found corner **2** is at (N 1,000.00, E 6,000.00) — a measured 5,000.00-ft line. The lost intermediate corner has a **record distance of 2,000.00 ft from corner 1** on a record line total of 5,000.00 ft. Restore its easting.

1. **Record fraction:** `2,000 / 5,000 = 0.40`.
2. **Restored E:** `E = E₁ + (E₂ − E₁) × 0.40 = 1,000 + (6,000 − 1,000) × 0.40 = 1,000 + 2,000 = 3,000.00 ft.`
3. Northing is unchanged here (the line is due east), so the restored corner is **(N 1,000.00, E 3,000.00).**

**Calculator:** `1000 + ( 6000 − 1000 ) × ( 2000 ÷ 5000 ) =` → **3,000**. This linear-interpolation form generalizes single proportion to any coordinate.

---

## Example 6 — Texas vara conversion (callout problem)

A Texas GLO field note calls **"S 45°00′ E, 950 vrs"** to a corner. Convert the distance to feet, and give the latitude/departure.

1. **Distance in feet:** `950 × 2.7778 = 2,638.9 ft` (or 950 ÷ 0.36 = 2,638.9 ft).
2. **Bearing S 45°00′ E → azimuth** = 180° − 45° = **135°**. Lat = 2,638.9 × cos135° = **−1,866.1 ft** (south); Dep = 2,638.9 × sin135° = **+1,866.1 ft** (east).

**Calculator:** `950 × 2.7778 =` → 2,638.9; then `× cos(135) =` → −1,866.1 and `× sin(135) =` → +1,866.1 (DEGREE mode). **Texas note:** the historic bearing is likely magnetic/assumed — a retracing surveyor must reconcile it to a modern datum (State Plane, NAD83) before plotting.

title: Exam Tips & Calculator Strategy
content:
## Strategy for the boundary area (the biggest block of points)

- **Treat Boundary Law as your point bank.** It is the **largest area (19–29 questions)** and most items are **definitions and short reasoning** you can answer in under a minute. On preview, sweep these first and bank them before the long COGO problems.
- **Memorize the dignity of calls cold:** *natural > artificial > adjoinder > course > distance > quantity*, **all yielding to intent and the original surveyor's footsteps.** Many questions are a single application of this ladder (e.g., "a call to a blazed oak controls over a conflicting bearing/distance").
- **Know the PLSS section snake (1 in the NE, 36 in the SE) and the aliquot acreage shortcuts** (forty = 40, quarter = 160, eighty = 80). These are guaranteed quick points.
- **Classify the corner before you act:** existent → obliterated (collateral evidence) → lost (proportion). Proportioning is **always a last resort**; the most-common trap answer says "immediately proportion" when an obliterated corner is recoverable from a bearing tree, fence, or testimony.
- **Match the discrepancy rule to the conveyance type:** **sequential → senior/junior (no proration)**; **simultaneous (platted) → apportion excess/deficiency.** Reversing these is the classic boundary trap.

## Aliquot / acreage calculator tricks

- **Aliquot area = chain-divide 640.** Each "half" = `÷ 2`, each "quarter" = `÷ 4`. So *S½ of NE¼ of SW¼* = `640 ÷ 2 ÷ 4 ÷ 4 = 20`. Faster and less error-prone than multiplying fractions.
- **Acre ↔ ft²:** divide ft² by **43,560** for acres; a forty checks as 1,320 × 1,320 = 1,742,400 ft² = 40 ac.
- **Chains:** keep work in chains when the record is in chains (1 ch = 66 ft; 10 sq ch = 1 ac) — it avoids large numbers, then convert at the end.

## Proportionate-measurement tricks

- **Single proportion is one multiply:** `d' = D_record × (L_measured / L_record)` — set up the ratio once, multiply each record interval. In coordinates it is **linear interpolation** between the two found corners by the record fraction — do it as `C₁ + (C₂ − C₁) × fraction` on the calculator.
- **Double proportion = do it twice** (N–S, then E–W) and combine. Recognize it whenever the lost corner is an **interior section corner controlled in four directions**.
- **Sanity-check direction:** the restored corner must fall *between* the controlling monuments and the surplus/deficiency must split per the record ratio — if a half ends up longer than the whole, you inverted the ratio.

## Texas (SIT) callouts

- **No PLSS in most of Texas** — Texas grants are **metes-and-bounds keyed to a GLO survey + abstract**, measured in **varas** (1 vara = 33⅓ in = 2.7778 ft; ÷0.36 for ft→vara). Convert varas before any COGO.
- **Footsteps doctrine is strong in Texas** (*Stafford v. King*): follow the original surveyor's monuments over inconsistent field-note calls. **Adverse possession in Texas is statutory** (Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code Ch. 16, the 3/5/10/25-year tracks), **not** the single common-law test — and the **§16.025 five-year track requires paying taxes.**

## Common traps

- **Quantity/area is the weakest call** — "containing 5.00 acres more or less" never controls over a monument or a course-and-distance.
- **Avulsion fixes, accretion moves** — a sudden flood does **not** shift the boundary; gradual accretion does.
- **A quitclaim conveys only what the grantor has** (no warranty); a **warranty deed** guarantees title.
- **Recording acts:** a **notice** state lets a later BFP-without-notice win even if recorded second; **race-notice** requires the BFP to also record first. Texas is a **pure notice** state.
- **Easements are non-possessory** and (if appurtenant) **pass with the land** — they cannot be conveyed separately from the dominant estate.

## How the handbook helps

The NCEES FS Reference Handbook v2.5 gives the **Land Description (PLSS) diagram**, the **unit conversions** (acre = 43,560 ft²; chain = 66 ft; mile = 80 chains), and the **area-by-coordinates** formula. Most boundary-law questions, though, are **conceptual** and not in the handbook — they reward *prepared knowledge* of the dignity of calls, senior/junior rights, water-boundary doctrine, and the BLM corner-restoration rules. Study those cold; use the handbook only for the conversions and the PLSS diagram.

title: Module Overview
content:
## Mapping the world, then building on it

**Mapping Processes and Methods** (14–21 of 110 questions) is the FS knowledge area that turns measurements into maps, and **photogrammetry, remote sensing, and GIS** are its high-yield computational and conceptual core. This module also reaches into **Surveying Processes** (construction layout, as-builts, quantities) and **Survey Computations** (earthwork volumes, slopes and grades), because the same student who can scale an aerial photo is expected to stake a building pad and compute the dirt to move.

**Photogrammetry** is the science of making measurements from photographs. From a single vertical aerial photo you can recover **scale** (`S = f/(H−h)`), correct for **relief displacement** (tall objects lean away from the photo center), and from a **stereo pair** you can measure heights via **parallax**. Modern practice replaces film with digital sensors, so the key map-resolution metric is now the **ground sample distance (GSD)** — the ground size of one pixel.

**Remote sensing** broadens this to non-photographic sensors: multispectral and hyperspectral satellite imagery, **LiDAR** (active laser ranging that yields dense 3-D point clouds and bare-earth DEMs), and **UAS/drone** platforms that have transformed small-area mapping.

**GIS** stores and analyzes spatial data in two models — **vector** (points/lines/polygons with attributes) and **raster** (a grid of cells) — and depends on correctly declared **projections, coordinate systems, and datums** (NAD83 horizontal, NAVD88 vertical) plus **metadata**. Mis-declared projections are the classic GIS blunder.

Finally, **construction surveying** lays the design back onto the ground: setting line and grade, computing **cut/fill** and **slope stakes**, and quantifying **earthwork** by the average-end-area and prismoidal formulas. Every formula here matches the **NCEES FS Reference Handbook v2.5** (Photogrammetry, Curvature & refraction, Earthwork sections) so the on-screen exam reference will look familiar.

![A vertical aerial photograph — the basic data of photogrammetry. Overlapping vertical photos are used to map planimetry and, in stereo, terrain elevations; photo scale S = f/H relates photo and ground distances.](/lessons/fs/photos/aerial-photo-usgs.jpg "Photo: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), public domain")

title: Key Concepts
content:
## Photogrammetry — vertical photo geometry

A **vertical aerial photograph** is taken with the camera axis (nearly) pointing straight down. The geometry is a perspective projection through the lens of **focal length f** at a **flying height H** above a datum; a point of ground height **h** sits at flying height **(H − h)** above it.

![An aerial view of the landscape. Photogrammetry turns overlapping aerial and UAV imagery into measurable maps, orthophotos, and elevation models.](/lessons/fs/photos/m8-survey-drone.jpg "Photo: Chensiyuan — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons")

- **Scale** of a vertical photo at a point of elevation h: `S = f / (H − h)`. Scale is a ratio (e.g., 1:6,000); it is **larger** (closer to 1) for low ground and high points, **smaller** for valleys. Use an **average scale** with `h = h_avg` for the whole photo.
- **Scale as a distance ratio:** `S = (photo distance) / (ground distance)`. So `ground distance = photo distance / S` and `photo distance = ground distance × S`. Keep f, H, and h in **consistent units** (convert f in mm to feet, or H to mm) before dividing.
- **Relief displacement** `d = r·h / H`: features above the datum are displaced **radially outward** from the principal point (photo center) by an amount proportional to the radial distance **r** and the object height **h**, and inversely to flying height **H**. This is why a building leans outward in an aerial photo — and the basis for measuring object heights from a single photo (`h = d·H/r`).

## Digital sensors and GSD

Digital cameras record a grid of pixels; the ground footprint of one pixel is the **ground sample distance**:

`GSD = (pixel size × H) / f`

with pixel size, H, and f in **consistent units**. A handy shortcut: **GSD(cm) = pixel(µm) × H(m) / [f(mm) × 10]**. Smaller GSD = higher resolution. Flight planning trades GSD against flying height and flight time.

## Stereo, overlap, and parallax

Aerial blocks are flown with ~**60% forward overlap** (endlap) and ~**30% sidelap** so every point appears on at least two photos, forming a **stereo model**. The horizontal distance between successive exposure stations is the **air base B**. **Parallax** `p = x − x′` is the difference in a point's photo position between the two images; greater parallax = closer to the camera = higher ground. Heights come from `h = H − f·B/p`, or differentially from `h₂ = h₁ + [(p₂ − p₁)/p₂]·(H − h₁)`.

## Remote sensing and LiDAR

- **Passive remote sensing** records reflected/emitted energy across spectral bands (visible, near-IR, thermal). **Multispectral/hyperspectral** imagery supports land-cover classification and vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI).
- **LiDAR** is **active** — it emits laser pulses and times the returns to build a dense 3-D **point cloud**. Multiple returns let it penetrate vegetation; classified ground returns produce a **bare-earth DEM**. Accuracy depends on GNSS/IMU positioning of the platform.
- **UAS/drones** carry cameras or small LiDAR for low-altitude, high-resolution mapping of small sites; products include orthomosaics, DSMs, and point clouds via **structure-from-motion (SfM)**.

## Maps, terrain models, and GIS data

- **Map scale** is the ratio of map distance to ground distance (1:1,200 means 1 unit on the map = 1,200 on the ground). **Contours** connect points of equal elevation; the **contour interval** is the vertical spacing.
- **Terrain models:** a **TIN** (triangulated irregular network) and **DEM/DSM** represent the surface; a **DSM** includes objects (canopy, buildings), a **DEM/DTM** is bare earth.
- **GIS data models:** **vector** stores discrete features (points, lines, polygons) with **attributes**; **raster** stores a continuous grid of cells (each holding a value). Vector is efficient for discrete boundaries; raster suits continuous phenomena (elevation, imagery).
- **Projections, coordinate systems, datums:** every spatial layer must declare its **projection** (Lambert Conformal Conic for E–W-extended states; Transverse Mercator for N–S states), **coordinate system** (e.g., SPCS), and **datum** (NAD83 horizontal, NAVD88 vertical; geoid undulation N relates ellipsoidal h to orthometric H via h = H + N). **Metadata** documents source, accuracy, and lineage. The #1 GIS failure is layers in mismatched/undeclared projections that don't overlay.

## Construction surveying

- **Stakeout (layout)** places stakes that mark horizontal position (line/offset) and vertical position (grade/cut-fill) for construction. Offset stakes sit a known distance from the feature so they survive excavation.
- **Grade** = the slope of a surface, usually expressed as a **percent**: `grade% = (ΔElev / horizontal distance) × 100`. A +2.0% grade rises 2 ft per 100 ft.
- **Cut and fill:** at a station, **cut** = existing − proposed (remove material); **fill** = proposed − existing (add material). **Slope stakes** mark where the design side slope (e.g., 2:1, run:rise) meets existing ground.
- **As-built (record) surveys** verify the finished work against design.

## Earthwork volumes

From cross-section **end areas** A₁, A₂ a distance L apart:

- **Average end area:** `V = L·(A₁ + A₂)/2` — simple, slightly overestimates for transitioning sections.
- **Prismoidal:** `V = L·(A₁ + 4·A_m + A₂)/6`, with A_m the area of the **mid-section** (not the average of A₁,A₂) — more accurate. Convert ft³ to **cubic yards** by ÷27. Apply **shrinkage** (fill compacts) or **swell** (excavated material bulks) factors as specified.

![Vertical aerial photo scale S = f / H′, where f is the camera focal length and H′ is the flying height above the ground being imaged. Ground distance = photo distance ÷ S.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/photo-scale.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![Aerial photo overlap: successive photos along a flight line share about 60% forward (end) lap so every ground point appears on at least two photos for stereo viewing; adjacent flight strips share about 30% side lap.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/stereo-overlap.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

![Reading a contour map: the interval is found from the spacing of the labeled index contours (every fifth line), then the highest (innermost) closed contour on the hill gives the summit contour elevation.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/contour-hill.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep (generated)")

![Tilted photograph geometry: the plumb line drops from the exposure station L to the ground nadir; the optical axis is perpendicular to the tilted photo through the principal point o; the principal line joins o and the photo nadir n.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/tilted-photo-geometry.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep (generated)")

![Sewer grade profile: the invert runs on a uniform grade between manholes; interpolating the flow line at a station and subtracting from the grade-stake elevation gives the cut.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/sewer-grade-profile.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep (generated)")

![Typical fill cross-section for slope staking: from the edge of road the side slope descends at s:1 to meet existing ground at the catch point; the catch-point offset from centerline = half-width + s·(fill height).](/lessons/fs/diagrams/cut-fill-section.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep (generated)")

title: Essential Formulas
content:
## Photogrammetry (vertical photos)

| Quantity | Formula | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Photo scale | `S = f / (H − h)` | f, H, h in consistent units; S is a ratio |
| Scale as distance ratio | `S = photo dist / ground dist` | |
| Ground distance | `D = d_photo / S = d_photo·(H − h)/f` | |
| Photo distance | `d_photo = D·S` | |
| Average scale | `S_avg = f / (H − h_avg)` | use mean ground elevation |
| Flying height above ground | `H − h = f / S` | invert the scale relation |
| Relief displacement | `d = r·h / H` | radial, outward from principal point |
| Object height from displacement | `h = d·H / r` | |

**Unit tip:** with f in millimeters and H, h in feet, convert f to feet first (`f_ft = f_mm/304.8`) or convert H to mm — never mix.

## Ground sample distance (digital sensors)

`GSD = (pixel size × H) / f`   (consistent units)

Shortcut: `GSD(cm) = pixel(µm) × H(m) / [f(mm) × 10]`

## Stereo / parallax

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Parallax | `p = x − x′` |
| Ground X, Y (parallax) | `X = x·B/p`,  `Y = y·B/p` |
| Height from parallax | `h = H − f·B/p` |
| Differential height | `h₂ = h₁ + [(p₂ − p₁)/p₂]·(H − h₁)` |
| Air base (ground units) | `B = (1 − endlap)·(ground width of photo)` |

(B = air base = ground distance between exposure stations; endlap ≈ 0.60, sidelap ≈ 0.30.)

## Map scale conversions

| Need | Relation |
|---|---|
| Ground from map | `ground = map dist × scale denominator` |
| Map from ground | `map dist = ground / scale denominator` |
| Engineer's scale 1 in = N ft | scale denominator = N × 12 |

## Grades and slopes

`grade % = (ΔElev / horizontal distance) × 100`     `ΔElev = grade × horizontal distance`

Side slope **s:1** (run:rise) means horizontal run = s × vertical rise.

## Earthwork volumes

| Method | Formula |
|---|---|
| Average end area | `V = L·(A₁ + A₂)/2` |
| Prismoidal | `V = L·(A₁ + 4·A_m + A₂)/6` |
| Pyramid/cone | `V = h·(base area)/3` |
| ft³ → yd³ | `÷ 27` |

## Height systems (mapping/GIS)

`h = H + N` — ellipsoidal height h, orthometric height H (NAVD88), geoid undulation N. Declare horizontal datum (NAD83) and vertical datum (NAVD88) in metadata.

---

## Example 1 — Photo scale of a vertical photograph

A vertical photo is taken with a **f = 152.4 mm** (6.00 in) camera from a flying height **H = 6,000 ft** above datum. The ground beneath averages **h = 1,000 ft**. Find the average scale.

1. Put f in feet: `f = 152.4 mm ÷ 304.8 = 0.500 ft` (6.00 in = 0.500 ft).
2. Flying height above the ground: `H − h = 6,000 − 1,000 = 5,000 ft`.
3. `S = f/(H − h) = 0.500 / 5,000 = 1/10,000`.

**Scale = 1:10,000** (1 in on the photo = 10,000 in = 833.3 ft on the ground).

**Calculator (TI-36X Pro):** `0.5 ÷ 5000 =` → `1×10⁻⁴`; take the reciprocal `x⁻¹` → **10,000**, so 1:10,000. **Casio fx-991:** identical. Watch the **unit conversion** of f from mm to ft — the single most common photogrammetry error.

---

## Example 2 — Ground distance from a photo measurement

On the photo of Example 1 (scale 1:10,000), two road intersections are **3.20 in** apart. What is their ground distance?

1. `ground = photo distance / S = 3.20 in × 10,000 = 32,000 in`.
2. `32,000 ÷ 12 = 2,666.7 ft`.

**Ground distance ≈ 2,666.7 ft.** Equivalently `D = d·(H − h)/f = 3.20 × 5,000 / 0.5 in`-consistent — keep units straight. **Calculator:** `3.2 × 10000 ÷ 12 =`.

---

## Example 3 — Ground sample distance (digital sensor)

A UAS camera has a **5.2 µm** pixel and **f = 24 mm** focal length, flown at **H = 400 m** above ground. Find the GSD.

1. Shortcut form: `GSD(cm) = pixel(µm) × H(m) / [f(mm) × 10] = 5.2 × 400 / (24 × 10)`.
2. `= 2,080 / 240 = 8.67 cm`.

**GSD ≈ 8.7 cm/pixel.** Check the full form: `GSD = (5.2×10⁻⁶ m × 400 m)/(0.024 m) = 0.0867 m = 8.67 cm`. ✓

**Calculator (Casio fx-991):** `5.2 × 400 ÷ ( 24 × 10 ) =` → 8.667. Confirm with the SI form using `×10^x` for the µm→m and mm→m conversions.

---

## Example 4 — Relief displacement

A radio tower images at radial distance **r = 4.50 in** from the principal point. Its top is **h = 500 ft** above the datum; flying height **H = 5,000 ft**. Find the relief displacement and the tower height if measured displacement is 0.45 in.

1. **Predicted displacement:** `d = r·h/H = 4.50 × 500 / 5,000 = 0.45 in` (the top leans 0.45 in outward from its base).
2. **Inverting to get height** from a measured `d = 0.45 in`: `h = d·H/r = 0.45 × 5,000 / 4.50 = 500 ft`. ✓

**Calculator:** `4.5 × 500 ÷ 5000 =` → 0.45. Relief displacement is **radial**, so always measure r and d from the **principal point**, not the photo corner.

---

## Example 5 — Flying height from a required scale

A mapping job specifies photos at **1:12,000** with a **f = 6.00 in (0.500 ft)** camera over flat ground at elevation **h = 0**. What flying height above the ground is required?

1. `H − h = f / S = 0.500 / (1/12,000) = 0.500 × 12,000 = 6,000 ft`.
2. With h = 0, the flying height above datum **H = 6,000 ft**.

**Flying height = 6,000 ft above ground.** **Calculator:** `0.5 × 12000 =`.

---

## Example 6 — Earthwork volume by average end area

Two adjacent cross-sections **100 ft apart** have end areas **A₁ = 220 ft²** and **A₂ = 380 ft²**. Find the cut volume in cubic yards.

1. `V = L·(A₁ + A₂)/2 = 100 × (220 + 380)/2 = 100 × 300 = 30,000 ft³`.
2. `÷ 27 = 1,111 yd³`.

**V ≈ 1,111 yd³.** If a mid-section area A_m = 305 ft² were given, the **prismoidal** result would be `V = 100·(220 + 4·305 + 380)/6 = 100·(1,820)/6 = 30,333 ft³ = 1,123 yd³`. **Calculator:** `100 × ( 220 + 380 ) ÷ 2 ÷ 27 =`.

title: Exam Tips & Calculator Strategy
content:
## Strategy for the mapping area

- **Photogrammetry items are mostly one-formula plug-ins** (`S = f/(H−h)`, `GSD`, `d = r·h/H`, map-scale ratios). They are fast points if you keep **units consistent** — convert f from mm to ft (÷304.8) or H from ft to mm before dividing. Budget ~2 min each and bank them.
- **GIS/remote-sensing/mapping concept questions are even faster** — vector vs. raster, datum/projection, LiDAR vs. passive, contour interval. These are recall points; answer them on sight and save calculator time for COGO.
- **Construction/earthwork items** reuse Module-5 skills: grade %, cut/fill, and the average-end-area/prismoidal volume formulas. Remember **÷27 for cubic yards** and the **A_m is the mid-section area, not the average**.

## Approved-calculator tricks (TI-36X Pro / Casio fx-991 / HP-35S)

- **Scale is a ratio:** compute `f/(H−h)` then press **x⁻¹** (reciprocal) to read the scale denominator (e.g., 1×10⁻⁴ → 10,000 → 1:10,000).
- **Unit conversions:** TI-36X Pro and Casio have a **convert/constants** menu, but it's faster to memorize `1 ft = 304.8 mm`, `1 m = 3.2808 ft`, `1 in = 25.4 mm`. Use **×10^x** for µm (×10⁻⁶) and mm (×10⁻³) in the GSD SI form.
- **GSD shortcut** avoids unit juggling entirely: `GSD(cm) = pixel(µm)·H(m)/[f(mm)·10]` — one keystroke chain.
- **Store the flying height** (STO) when several photo-scale parts share the same H to avoid re-keying.
- **Earthwork:** chain `L×(A₁+A₂)÷2÷27` in one expression; use the calculator's fraction/parenthesis entry to avoid order-of-operations slips.

## Common traps

- **Mixing units in the scale formula** — f in mm but H in ft. Convert first. This is the #1 photogrammetry mistake.
- **Scale direction:** scale gets **larger** (denominator smaller) for **higher** ground (smaller H−h). Hilltops are at larger scale than valleys on the same photo.
- **Relief displacement is radial** — r and d are measured from the **principal point**, and the displacement is **outward** for points above the datum.
- **Average end area vs. prismoidal:** A_m is the **mid-section** area, NOT (A₁+A₂)/2. Average-end-area slightly **overestimates**; the prismoidal correction reduces it.
- **Cubic yards:** divide ft³ by **27**, not 9. And watch shrinkage (compacted fill needs *more* bank volume) vs. swell.
- **Datum vs. projection vs. coordinate system** are three different things in GIS — a layer needs all three declared to overlay correctly; geoid undulation N links ellipsoidal and orthometric heights (h = H + N).
- **DSM vs. DEM/DTM:** DSM includes objects (canopy, buildings); DEM/DTM is bare earth — LiDAR last-return/ground-classified points give the DEM.

## How the handbook helps

The NCEES FS Reference Handbook v2.5 lists the **Photogrammetry** block (scale `f/(H−h)`, relief displacement `r·h/H`, parallax forms, flying height) and the **Earthwork** block (average end area, prismoidal, pyramid) verbatim, plus **Conversions** (ft↔m, in↔mm, acre, the 43,560 and 27 factors). Know *where* the Photogrammetry and Earthwork sections sit in the Mathematical & Surveying-Related Formulas chapter so you can confirm a formula in seconds rather than deriving it under time pressure.

title: Module Overview
content:
## Speed is a skill — and it is the cheapest points on the FS

![An NCEES-approved scientific calculator. Fluency with DMS entry, rectangular↔polar conversion, and memory registers is worth real points and minutes on exam day.](/lessons/fs/photos/m9-scientific-calculator.jpg "Photo: Jphill19 — CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons")

The FS gives you **110 questions in 5 hours 20 minutes — about 2.9 minutes each**. The boundary-law, ethics, and definition items are fast if you know them, but the computational questions (Survey Computations and Applied Math, ~27–41 of the 110) are where time *bleeds*. A surveyor who fumbles a DMS entry, hunts for the polar-conversion key, or hand-cranks an inverse with atan and quadrant bookkeeping will run out of clock before running out of knowledge. A surveyor whose calculator is an extension of their hand banks those points and buys time for the harder items. **Calculator fluency is the single highest-leverage exam skill that costs nothing but practice.**

This module is not new theory — Modules 4 and 5 already taught the COGO, traverse, area, and curve formulas. Here you learn to **execute** them at speed on an **NCEES-approved calculator**, and to spend the time you save wisely with deliberate test strategy.

## The 2026 approved-calculator list

NCEES limits you to a fixed list, **re-issued every year** (same list for FS, FE, PS, PE). **No programmable, graphing, or CAS calculators.** For **2026**:

- **Casio** — all **fx-115** and **fx-991** models (the name must contain "fx-115" or "fx-991").
- **Hewlett Packard** — **HP 33s** and **HP 35s** only (no other HP).
- **Texas Instruments** — all **TI-30X** and **TI-36X** models (the name must contain "TI-30X" or "TI-36X").

**Buy and master one of two:** the **TI-36X Pro** (the most-recommended FS/FE calculator — DMS, polar↔rectangular, matrices, stats, solver, two-line MathPrint display) or the **Casio fx-991EX ClassWiz** (fast, large display, excellent DMS/stat, TABLE mode). The HP 33s/35s are **discontinued** and use RPN — great for COGO chaining if you already love RPN, but not worth learning from scratch. **Always confirm the current year's list on ncees.org before your exam**, and bring a **second approved calculator** as a backup.

title: Key Concepts
content:
## The five operations every surveyor must own

Master these and you can solve almost every FS computational item quickly:

1. **DMS entry & arithmetic** — type, add, and subtract angles in degrees-minutes-seconds.
2. **DMS ↔ decimal degrees** — convert in one keystroke, both directions.
3. **Rectangular → polar (R▸P)** — turns (ΔE, ΔN) into (distance, angle): the **inverse** in one step.
4. **Polar → rectangular (P▸R)** — turns (distance, azimuth) into (ΔE, ΔN): the **forward** in one step.
5. **Memory registers** — STO/RCL (and SUM where available) to chain a traverse without re-keying coordinates.

## DMS entry, arithmetic, and conversion

Survey angles are **degrees-minutes-seconds** (e.g., 257°44′10″). Both approved families convert and compute in DMS natively, so you never have to hand-convert.

- **TI-36X Pro:** the angle key is **[2nd][DMS]** (the `°′″` menu). Enter `257°44′10″` as `257 [2nd][DMS]°  44 [2nd][DMS]′  10 [2nd][DMS]″`. To **convert a decimal to DMS**, compute the value then `[2nd][DMS] → ▸DMS`. To go **DMS → decimal**, just enter the DMS value and the calculator already stores it as decimal internally.
- **Casio fx-991EX:** the key is **[°′″]**. Enter `257 [°′″] 44 [°′″] 10 [°′″]`. Pressing **[°′″]** again (or `SHIFT [°′″]` → `▸DMS`) toggles the **answer** between decimal degrees and D°M′S″.
- **HP-33S/35S:** store angles as **H.MMSSss** and convert with **→HR** (HMS→decimal) and **→HMS** (decimal→HMS).
- **Arithmetic in DMS:** you can add/subtract angles directly — e.g., balancing interior angles, or summing a deflection. Enter each angle in DMS and press `+`/`−`; the result displays in DMS (or convert as needed). Keep the calculator in **DEGREE (DEG) mode** so all trig uses degrees.

## Why R▸P / P▸R is the heart of COGO

A survey leg has two equivalent descriptions: **rectangular** (ΔE, ΔN) = (departure, latitude), and **polar** (distance, direction). The calculator's built-in conversions move between them **in one step**, replacing a whole chain of `√`, `atan`, and quadrant logic:

- **Inverse** (two coordinates → distance + azimuth): compute `ΔE = E₂ − E₁` and `ΔN = N₂ − N₁`, feed them to **R▸P**, and read **distance** and **azimuth** directly. The calculator's R▸P returns the angle measured from the x-axis with the correct sign — combine with the handbook quadrant constant (or use `atan2`) to land in 0–360° azimuth.
- **Forward** (point + azimuth + distance → new coordinates): feed **distance** and **azimuth** to **P▸R** and read **ΔE (departure)** and **ΔN (latitude)** directly, then add to the start point. This *is* `ΔN = D·cos(Az)`, `ΔE = D·sin(Az)` done in one operation.

**Convention used here (matches the RPLS notes):** treat **x = ΔE (Easting/departure)** and **y = ΔN (Northing/latitude)**, with the angle measured as an **azimuth from north**. Some calculators define the polar angle from the x-axis; if yours does, enter ΔN as x and ΔE as y (or swap the read-out) so the angle comes out as an azimuth. Drill *your own* unit until you know which slot is which without thinking.

## Angle modes — keep it in DEG

Set the calculator to **DEGREE (DEG)** mode and confirm the **DEG** indicator before any trig. A calculator left in **RAD** or **GRAD** is the classic silent blunder — answers will be wildly wrong with no error message. Curve, traverse, and inverse work all assume degrees.

## Memory registers — chain a traverse

Use **STO/RCL** (TI: `[sto→]`/`[rcl]`; Casio: `[STO]`/`[RCL]` with variables A,B,C,…,X,Y,M) to hold running Northing and Easting totals so you never re-key a coordinate. On the TI-30Xa the **[SUM+]** key accumulates a value into memory — the basis of the leg-by-leg traverse routine in Part B. Store a constant like the vertical-curve parabola term or a fixed radius once, then reuse it. **Every value you re-key is a chance for a blunder; store it instead.**

## Fractions, reciprocals, and other time-savers

- **Reciprocal `x⁻¹`** reads a scale denominator (e.g., `f/(H−h)` then `x⁻¹`) or converts relative precision to a 1:N ratio.
- **Fraction entry** (TI MathPrint, Casio Natural display) lets you type `(A₁+A₂)/2` as a stacked fraction, avoiding order-of-operations slips.
- **Ans** recalls the last result to chain calculations; **parentheses** protect order of operations in long expressions.
- **Stat mode** (mean, sample σ) handles repeated-measurement and error-propagation items without summing by hand.

![Converting between degrees-minutes-seconds and decimal degrees: dd = D + M/60 + S/3600, and back. Set the calculator to DEG mode and carry full precision until the final answer.](/lessons/fs/diagrams/dms-conversion.svg "Original diagram — Starr SIT Prep")

The statistics registers are worth the ten minutes it takes to learn them properly.

title: Essential Formulas
content:
## Each survey task → the calculator operation that solves it

| Survey task | Math | Calculator operation |
|---|---|---|
| Convert a field angle to decimal | `dec = D + M/60 + S/3600` | enter in **DMS**, read decimal (toggle) |
| Convert a decimal answer to DMS | — | **▸DMS** (TI `[2nd][DMS]`, Casio `SHIFT[°′″]`) |
| Add/subtract angles | balance / deflection sums | enter each in **DMS**, `+` / `−` |
| **Inverse** (two pts → distance) | `D = hypot(ΔN, ΔE)` | **R▸P**, read r |
| **Inverse** (two pts → azimuth) | `Az = (toDeg(atan2(ΔE,ΔN)) + 360) mod 360` | **R▸P**, read θ, then quadrant constant |
| **Forward** (az+dist → coords) | `ΔN = D·cos(Az)`, `ΔE = D·sin(Az)` | **P▸R**, read ΔE and ΔN |
| Bearing → azimuth | quadrant rule (below) | mental + DMS |
| Azimuth → bearing | quadrant rule (below) | mental + DMS |
| Back azimuth | `Az_back = (Az + 180) mod 360` | `±180` |
| Area from coordinates | `A = ½·|Σ(Xᵢ·Y_{i+1} − X_{i+1}·Yᵢ)|` | sum of cross-products, ÷2, abs |
| Curve tangent | `T = R·tan(I/2)` | DEG mode, `tan(I/2)` |
| Curve length | `L = R·I·(π/180)` | `R × I × π ÷ 180` or `(I/D)·100` |

## Bearing ↔ azimuth quadrant rules (memorize)

Azimuth runs **0–360° clockwise from north**. A bearing is a **quadrant letter + acute angle β**:

| Quadrant | Bearing → Azimuth | Azimuth → Bearing |
|---|---|---|
| **NE** (Az 0–90) | `Az = β` | `N β E` |
| **SE** (Az 90–180) | `Az = 180 − β` | `S (180−Az) E` |
| **SW** (Az 180–270) | `Az = 180 + β` | `S (Az−180) W` |
| **NW** (Az 270–360) | `Az = 360 − β` | `N (360−Az) W` |

The **sign of ΔN and ΔE** fixes the quadrant on an inverse: ΔN+/ΔE+ → NE; ΔN−/ΔE+ → SE; ΔN−/ΔE− → SW; ΔN+/ΔE− → NW.

## Inverse — the azimuth, robustly

The one-line bare-helper form that always lands in 0–360°:

`Az = (toDeg(atan2(ΔE, ΔN)) + 360) − 360·floor((toDeg(atan2(ΔE, ΔN)) + 360)/360)`

Note the argument order **atan2(ΔE, ΔN)** — easting first, northing second — because azimuth is measured from north (the ΔN axis). On the calculator, R▸P does this for you; the formula is the fallback when you key it by hand.

## DMS as total seconds (handy for drills/precision)

`total seconds = D·3600 + M·60 + S`, and back: `D = floor(sec/3600)`, `M = floor((sec mod 3600)/60)`, `S = sec mod 60`.

## Combined-factor and other one-key chains

- **Grid from ground:** `grid = ground × combined factor`; **ground from grid:** `ground = grid / combined factor`. Store the combined factor, multiply/divide.
- **Scale denominator:** compute the ratio, press `x⁻¹`.
- **Relative precision:** `misclosure ÷ perimeter`, then `x⁻¹` for 1:N.
